subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The House resumed from' Tuesday, May 30, the debate on the motion of Hon. W. S. Fielding (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. Sir Henry Drayton.
Mr. A. W. NEILL, (Comox-Alberni) : Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to waste the time of the House listening to me expounding my views on the tariff. In the opinion of one or two hon. members of this House-I hope it is only one or two-my views on that subject are both crude and unorthodox. Probably they are, Sir, but at least they are my own, founded on conditions as I have myself observed them, and not inherited from my parents or from the traditions of some half-worn-out party. They at least possess one saving grace, and that is they afford wide tolerance of the views of any other hon. gentlemen who hold different views from my own. They afford any other hon. member ample opportunity to differ from me on this subject without my feeling called upon to reflect upon his mental capacity or moral standing, which I see by the debates of this House some hon. members are rather in the habit of doing.
At the beginning of this session I laid it down as an axiom that the discussion of free [trade and ^protection ofBers ample scope for interminable argument on both sides of the question, and the longer I sit in this House the more convinced I am that that axiom is absolutely correct. Everything can be said on one side and everything can be said on the other side. I do think, however, that we are rather in danger of making a fetish out of this question of the tariff. After all, it is not a question of principle: it is a question of fact and policy. I think some of us at least are rather apt to elevate what is only a matter of opinion into a matter of moral standards, and make it a matter of moral principle from which it is improper for any one to deviate. I repeat that it is not a question or right or wrong. It ds a question of opinion. An hon. gentleman who spoke the other day referred somewhat slightingly to a statement I made earlier in the session, that because I lived in British Columbia I advocated protection, but that I had no doubt if I lived on the prairies I would be advocating free trade. It seemed to him that that was somewhat derogatory. After all, Mr. Speaker, I only said that I would do what every other hon. member does without saying so; that is an absolute fact. I certainly said that the tariff was a matter simply of geography, and that because I was in British Columbia I believed in a tariff policy for British Columbia. In British Columbia we do not, most of us at any rate, steal from, or rob our neighbours, not to any appreciable extent, but we do not do that simply because we live in British Columbia. If we moved to Manitoba we would neither rob nor steal there, because that is a question of moral standards by which honourable men are bound. It has nothing to do with the tariff, and because I advocate protection in British Columbia I fail entirely to see why I should not advocate free trade in Manitoba. Here is a fair example of the difference between the two.
In the part of the province of British Columbia from which I come, it has been found appropriate and most successful to plant potatoes at a certain period of the year, we will say the first of May, and we invariably follow that practice because we have found it appropriate to the conditions. If we moved down to Manitoba where experience had shown that it was wise to plant potatoes six weeks earlier perhaps, would I receive any applause from hon. members because I then took the position: No, I have planted potatoes always on the 1st day of May; I will not lower the flag that I have lived under for twenty years, of planting my potatoes on that date; I will go on doing so. I think I would get little applause, and still fewer potatoes. I will go further and say that not only
The Budget-Mr. Neill

do I believe it is right for me to advocate protection for British Columbia; but I believe it is also right for hon. gentlemen to my left to advocate free trade for the prairies, because presumably experience has shown that that is the policy best adapted to that district. The only dispute which will arise between us is when hon. gentlemen to my left try to convince me that free trade 'is the policy for British Columbia. Then we shall get into a dispute. Once we accept the fact that certain sections of this country from their geographical position and economic conditions want, some free trade, and some a tariff, all we have left to do then is to formulate a tariff policy, not that will attempt to give every section what it wants, but as far as possible will be a compromise between the different sections. The tariff is always a compromise. Then our only question to consider to-day is, have we-* British Columbia in my case, the prairies in the case of hon. gentlemen to my left 

got such a measure of justice out of this tariff compromise as we are entitled to? Any further remarks I make on the tariff to-day will be along that line.
The budget is a compromise. I think the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) will take no exception to that. It is a compromise, as I said in my election campaign months ago that it would be, and I believe that the only question for us to discuss to-day is whether that compromise is fair to the different sections we represent. The budget has been so fully discussed the past few days in this House, and there are leaders much more competent to discuss it than I am, that I shall not touch further on it. I only wish this afternoon to consider the question for a few minutes from one angle, and that is the angle of British Columbia. I would not have spoken on this subject at all except that I did not want to give a silent vote. I do not believe in ambiguity of thought, word, or deed, and therefore, Mr. Speaker, I will frankly and plainly say now that I intend to vote against the amendment moved by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), and on the main question of the budget resolutions I intend to support once again the Government. I will say with equal frankness that I have very grave doubt and hesitation in my mind whether in doing so I am acting in the best interests of the constituency I represent or of the province that I come from. I somewhat suspect that my constituents may share that doubt and hesita-
'Mr. Neill.]
tion, and it is for that reason I wish to go on record explaining briefly the position I take here to-day.
After the election last December, when it was shown what the complexion of this House would be, I consulted with my friends throughout the riding as to what attitude it would be proper for me to take in this House and we arrived at the decision that being elected as an Independent, being a new member in a new Parliament, and with a new Government, it would be proper, provided the Government introduced reasonably -suitable legislation, which was to be supposed, that I should support them for at least one session in order to give them an opportunity to set their house in order, formulate their plans, and bring down a programme which might or might not meet our views then. I may say that had the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) been the leader of the Government, or had a coalition been formed which included that hon. gentleman, we would have taken the same attitude, that is to say, we would have given them a reasonable opportunity for one session to show what their programme would be. In pursuance of that attitude I have supported the Government through this entire session, with one exception, and that was on the Asiatic question, when the question was too great and too important to British Columbia for me to deviate from what I believed to be -the exact necessities of the case. I hold no mandate for the other members from British Columbia, and I have no right to traverse their motives, but the records of the House -are before us and I can see from them that the other members from British Columbia, except the Conservative members, have practically -supported the Government solidly during this session. It is not for me to traverse their motives, but presumably they were actuated by some -such idea as animated myself and my friends. -So we find the situation is this, that practically fifty per cent of the representation of British Columbia, six at least out of thirteen, have given strong support to the Government of the day during this session, no doubt with the idea that if their policy continued to meet with the approval of their constituents they might continue that support; and also, no doubt, with the ulterior idea on the part of the government that if their policy, as developed, was suitable to the districts we represent, then, in the event of an election, they would secure greater support from the members from

The Budget-Mr. Neill
British Columbia. That, Mr. Speaker, was the fond dream that we, in our political youth and innocence, brought down to this House. It has been said:
There's nothing half so sweet in life
As love's young dream.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, and I am sorry to say there is nothing so bitter and complete as the disillusion that sometimes follows "love's young dream." Let us canvass for a moment what the results are. The session is drawing to its close and from my point of view the only members from British Columbia that will be going home with a cheerful countenance and a glad heart will be those representing the Conservative cities of British Columbia. And, why indeed, should they not have a glad heart? They have excellent reasons for it, and those reasons are furnished by the government that sits opposite us to-day. In the first place they have succeeded in getting huge sums of money for their constituencies, very large votes. It may have escaped the notice of hon. members that the whole of the vote for public buildings for British Columbia, and it is a very considerable sum, is to be spent in the cities of British Columbia

Victoria and Vancouver. There is a vote for William's Head. That is a little outside of Victoria, but it practically means that city because the money will be spent there, and the men to be employed will be from that city; so that the whole of the vote for public buildings in British Columbia goes to the two cities of Victoria and Vancouver. I say to the representatives of those cities: Well done. I am not casting any reflection on them. In addition to that, Victoria gets a few million dollars-I do not know the exact amount, I think it will be millions- for the continuation of its dry dock. Vancouver is also to get its dry dock. Possibly it has not yet been decided on; but the members from there have only got to continue as they are doing, attack the Government a little more, move a few more votes of want of confidence, and I have no doubt they too will get their dry dock. I may say that I had the opportunity of seeing an election address brought out by one of the candidates for the city of Vancouver at the last election, and he made it quite plain that he had been instrumental more or less in obtaining in four years for the city of Vancouver expenditures amounting to something like $5,000,000. I have no doubt his statement was correct, at least I am not prepared to dispute it; and it 147J
surely is very much to his credit as a representative that he was able to get an expenditure of something like a million and a quarter every year for the comparatively small city of Vancouver. May I be allowed to offer the suggestion that people who have been getting public expenditure at the rate of a million and a quarter a year for a number of years past might perhaps have taken a holiday in expenditure this session and allowed some of the money to go where it was really, perhaps, more needed. It may be said that this is none of my business. As I say I am not attacking these gentlemen at all; the more credit to them for their ability in securing these sums; but what does interest me is the question: Who is furnishing this money, and where does it come from? It may be said: "It comes from the public exchequer; what matters that to you?" Yes, Mr. Speaker, it comes from the public exchequer but it is also diverted from where it should be spent, and that is the rural constituencies of British Columbia. It is well known that only a certain amount of money will be voted to any province in a given time; and when that money is spent by the million in certain cities in the province it is obvious that no money will be available for the rural constituencies of that province; and that is exactly what has happened, and is going to happen, in the case of British Columbia. Now in the past, that policy has gone on for many years; it has not been so obvious, for the simple reason that the rural constituencies in previous years have been so ill advised as to elect city representatives, representatives living in the cities of Victoria and Vancouver. For twelve years at least the member for the riding that I now represent lived and had his business interests in Vancouver; and he was not likely to stand up here and object to a few additional contracts going into that city where he had all his interests. The same thing applies to other cities in British Columbia and, no doubt, applies to other provinces. The country sections have now awakened, and they have decided to send men, as in the case of the gentlemen to my left, who really and truly represent not only their own interests but their own constituencies; and the result is there is going to be a howl go up from the country districts of British Columbia at all the money being voted and distributed in the city municipalities.
I might mention incidentally-and let me say that I want to keep away from all petty or parochial politics-that the popu-
The Budget-Mr. Neill

lation of the district that I represent has increased, according to the last census, 33 or 36 per cent, and there is no other riding in the province of British Columbia where the population has increased to that extent, and it is one of the largest there, except the riding of South Vancouver, which is largely urban. Some of the other constituencies that are dragging down these big votes, have increased only 7 per cent in the same period. It can be readily understood that a district as large as that, growing at the rate I have indicated, must have ever-increasing needs in the way of wharves and lights for navigation, and so on; much more so than a stagnant city whose population only increased 7 per cent in the same period. The resources of British Columbia are to a large extent undeveloped. They are not to be found in the cities but in the country districts; and if you do not develop the country districts your cities will not make very rapid progress.
Another reason why the Conservative members of British Columbia should go home with a glad heart is the fact that the Government, unwittingly I should suppose, has furnished them with the very best of campaign material for the next election. They have put it in the power of these hon. gentlemen to go home to their constituencies, and to other constituencies and say: "I told you so; the Government have done exactly what we said they would do if they got into power." I would not say they have done it all, because the statements made by some Conservative candidates went too far altogether; but they are in a position to say, "I told you that you would suffer from the tariff; that you would suffer in this way and that way." Every opportunity has been given to them to do so. I do not need to imagine that such a claim would be made because we heard the hon. member for Yale (Mr. MacKelvie) saying the other day that the doing away, as it practically is, of the dumping clause on fruit was very much to his interest politically; but he was man enough to go on and say that he did not wish to take advantage of that. He would be willing to forego that, that is the way he put it, if the Government would change back to the old policy in the interests of his constituency; but the fact that the dumping clause has practically been done away with is virtually an election by acclamation for him at the next election. Therefore I say that those hon. gentlemen are going home with a glad heart rather than those men who supported the Government.

Now let me consider for a moment, very briefly, what the rural sections of British Columbia have obtained during this session.
Not only the rural districts, but all the districts, of British Columbia by almost unanimous vote asked the Government for the exclusion of orientals and we got- promises, it is true, promises-promises that cannot under any circumstances fructify into legislation for another twelve months, a sort of political promissory note, dated a year ahead and always subject to be renewed then. What we did want at that time, and what we want now, is action -immediate, prompt and decisive action. I may say that even since that debate on the exclusion of orientals took place in the House another aspect of it has come to my attention to which I would like to invite the consideration of the House. I have here British Columbia's Lumber Journal and, under date of April 20, we find the following in it:
Valuable timber tracts on Vancouver Island are likely to pass into Japanese ownership in the near future, according to reports in circulation here. It is said that Hon. Samuel Hill, Seattle millionaire, who recently returned from Japan, is extensively interested in Alberni Canal timber limits and that he is negotiating for a sale of a big block of this timber to Japanese interests. Another deal is now being handled by a Victoria real estate firm, it being understood that the prospective buyers are lumber importers oif Kobe. In the event of the sales being put through, the Japanese would probably establish their own logging camps and mills, cut the logs into big-dimension timber suitable for export and ship it across to Japan in Japanese freighters.
Further on a lumber merchant from this same Tokio, Japan, says:
"British Columbia lumbermen should not think that the Japanese market is merely a flash in the pan-here to-day and gone to-morrow. If my estimate is worth anything, Japan will be in the market for British Columbia lumber, just as long as British Columbia has lumber to sell.'*
I ask hon. members to notice this next sentence:
"The Japanese government has prohibited the cutting of lumber in most of our native forests, and consequently we must get our supplies elsewhere."
Observe the shrewdness and the foresightedness of the Japanese government. They have prohibited the exploiting of their own forests at the present time and forced them to come to our forests to get their lumber, and that is all right, because we want to sell our lumber. That shows their foresightedness, because they want to protect their own forests. I have here a

The Budget-Mr. Neill
memorandum of the loadings of lumber shipped from British Columbia, and I find the following took place in less than one month.
From Alberni the Canadian Prospector was loaded with lumber for the Orient; the Canadian Farmer was loaded with lumber for California, and the Canadian Winner was loaded with lumber for the Orient. From Chemalnus the Canadian Freighter and the Canadian Prospector were loaded with lumber for the Orient.
Four government boats, besides other boats, left our shores with lumber inside of three weeks, and the Japs are going to do away with it all. The Japanese government has become aware of the business we were doing, and they are going to buy up our lumber, and have it cut by their own men, and ship it in their own bottoms. I think history tells us that Nero fiddled while Rome was burning. In a different sense and in a less worthy sense we are "fiddling" whilst Japan is buying our raw resources, and pouring in her nationals to exploit them, and we get nothing but the bare original cost of the raw material. That is why we are asking for urgent action. I was saying that we asked for exclusion of orientals, and only got promises from the Government. But, in justice to the Government, it may be asked "What did you get from the previous government?" I do not know whether we got as liberal promises as we have received from the hon. members opposite, but the comparison does not prevail. There are two arguments against that which show that is not a just comparison. One is that the fact that the late government had not acted along these lines proved a very considerable factor against their candidates in the last election, and was a no mean factor in their defeat in the country districts in British Columbia: the public said "We do not like this lack of action; we will send men to parliament pledged to take some action." Therefore it is not sufficient to say "Well the late government did not do any better either", because our constituents and the public expect something to be done in the near future.
There we have the oriental question, and we will take the working man now. I believe it is not popular here to refer to the working man, but we are going home by and by and we will come in contact with him. He asked for an eight hour day, and he was told by the provincial government that it was a matter for the Dominion and not for the provinces. He was told it had some connection with the Treaty of Versailles and he was entitled to have
it. I think that it formed no inconsiderable plank in the Liberal platform, I am speaking subject to correction as to that, but we came here and reiterated the demand made by our constituents, and we were told that it was not a matter of Dominion legislation but a matter of provincial legislation. That may be; I do not gainsay that statement. There was a suggestion and an inquiry made in the House, would the Government not call the representatives of the various provinces together, and have a conference with a view to passing legislation by all the different provinces, so that the matter would be adjusted? And we were given no assurance that it would be done. Further than that, the Government itself has fallen down and refused to carry out this principle on its own public work. I consider we are more or less obligated to do this under our treaty obligation. So much for that aspect of the case.
The next item I draw attention to comes under the tariff, and this matter, as I said, is a compromise, a sort of political grab bag. Each province and each interest shuts its eyes and puts in its hand and sees what it will bring out, and some of the things they succeed in getting are quite out of keeping with the needs of the people who draw them. You often see the same thing at a ladies' aid sale.
The lumber industry wants one thing and that only-and my hon. friends from British Columbia will agree with me in this-they want a reduction of high freight rates. They do not care about the tariff, if they can only get a reduction on the freight rates. Those mills situated on the water where they can ship their products are not so badly off, but there is a number of them situated inland; the only way they can ship is by train to the prairies and they cannot sell the lumber at a profit, after paying the freight. They come down asking for a reduction in the freight, and what do they get? They get 2h per cent reduction on their new machinery. I am not deprecating that at all1, beCause 21 per cent on a mill that would cost $100,000 to equip amounts to a very considerable sum; but the irony of the thing is that they do not want new machinery, because their present machinery is lying rusting by reason of the fact that they have not the freight rate necessary to take the timber out. When a man wants bread what is the use of offering him a stone? And until he can make the wheels of his present machinery turn it is little use to say that
The Budget-Mr. Neill
he can get a rebate if he buys machinery. It is a reduction in theory but not in effect.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In the Crows-nest Pass agreement is there a provision relating to lumber?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, lumber is not mentioned in that agreement.
I come now to the coal mining question. The coal miners ask protection-and I am not ashamed to use the word'-against the importation of fuel oil from the American side, and ask for an opportunity to work more than two days a week-that is all they are working now. You hear a great deal about the big wages they make but if they only work two days a week how much does it come to? At present they are only working two days a week, and they receive $40 a month. In my opinion that is not as much as $25 a month in Ontario, because the cost of living is so much higher out there. And these men are expected to live, have their homes, raise their fami-_ lies on $40 a month and pay high taxation.' The inspectors appointed under the British Columbia Minimum Wage Act have decided that $65 a month is the minimum sum that a girl in business can live decently on, and it is provided by law that she cannot be paid less than $65 a month. But the coal miner is expected to keep his wife and family and feed and clothe them on $40 a month, and that is all they are receiving at the present time in these mines. What do they get out of the political grab bag? They get nothing. They did get something. They got a vision of their own Canadian Merchant Marine going over three or four thousand miles to Japan and buying Japan coal mined by Japanese, and bringing it over, and selling it at the doors of our own coal mines, where the men are working only two days a week. How the Japanese authorities must laugh to see us sitting here passing resolutions, as solemnly as a lot of children playing at church, about restrictions and so on, and our very own Government boats are bringing Japan coal over to the detriment of our own workers out there in British Columbia. More than that, I claim the Government has not kept faith on this subject. I put a question on the order paper some time ago and drew the attention of the Government to the fact that a Canadian Government boat had gone over to Japan and brought a load of coal. After bringing the matter to the attention of the Government, I asked if this policy would be discontinued, and in reply, there was a positive assurance that,

so far as it was possible to do so-I think those were the words used-the practice would be discontinued. I sent that word home to those coal miners, and I assured them that at least this would not happen again. Only a few hours ago, however, I received this telegram from Cumberland, signed by the President of the Board of Trade:
Another shipment Japanese coal brought by C.G.S.S. Inventor transferred to Britisher. Britisher was due here for coal but had order cancelled result no work in mines to-day do not consider this good business for Canadian industries.
Neither do I. I will go further than that and say that that is an insult to our Canadian workers, a disgrace to the Canadian government, and incidentally a reflection upon ourselves. Those men who are not working are not Hungarians nor Poles; they are British-born miners, and they are the men about whom some hon. gentlemen waxed so eloquent the other day in the discussion about oleomargarine when they said that we must maintain at any hazard the right of the poor man to buy a cheap, spurious imitation of butter. Is there not a more potent right than that, the right of the poor man to have employment? I have cited this quotation before, but I will quote again what one of the leaders of the British government said in a debate in the House of Commons in London:
The classes who had the running of the country would be Judged in proportion as they could find or organize employment for the great mass of the people.
The word "people" in this connection means the people of Canada, not the people of Japan. That is the situation to-day, that these men are working two days a week, and we ourselves, for it is we, are bringing coal over from Japan. I might also mention incidentally that quite a large number of orientals are working in these mines with the full sanction and authority of law. They are dangerous; they are ignorant of our language; in case of an explosion or accident, they would add trebly to the danger and difficulties of the white men who are employed there. They are keeping out white men there to-day, and they, I suppose, are getting their two days' work a week. If the white men took the law into their own hands and broke out into open rioting, they would be promptly and properly punished, because the law must be observed. But if anything of that kind happened, would not some portion of the blame rest upon this Government and

The Budget-Mr. Neill
this House which, if not directly, have indirectly sanctioned conditions that prevail there to-day? I do not think we would be altogether clear from some blame attaching to ourselves. That is the situation as regards the coal industry. That is what the coal miners got out of this budget.
As regards the fishing industry, the fishermen asked for the elimination of purse seines and traps, and they also asked incidentally that the fishing should be limited to white men. What did they draw out of the budget? They drew a most extraordinary thing. They drew a substantial rebate on gasoline, and that reduction looked fair on the face of it, because fishermen use power boats. But the joker in this reduction is that the majority of them have motor power boats that do not use gasoline, and this reduction will be of practically no benefit to them. I imagine that, at the most, about ten per cent of them use gasoline, and the rest of them are not benefited one particle by this reduction in the budget. In some districts they are not allowed to use power boats. It was intended for fishermen; it was said so in the speech of the minister; but it does not benefit them, for the reasons I have stated.
The dairy industry asked for, not a tariff [protection, 'but simply a /protection against what they claimed was an unfair competition. I will not go into that again, because I have already discussed it. But the dairy industry is in a very critical condition to-day, and some form of protection was requested. What did the dairy industry get out of the budget? The ingredients that go into oleomargarine are allowed in free, although they are taxed if used for anything else, and in the budget we also find that free importation is provided for cottolene, which is a mess made of cottonseed oil and which is a sort of step-sister to oleomargarine. That is what the dairymen got out of the budget.
The fruit industry apparently only asked to be left alone. The fruit men did not appear to want anything; they seemed to say: "Just leave us alone." They had a dumping clause that protected them. If that dumping clause has not been removed, it has been changed to a method which they consider makes it absolutely unworkable. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) was discussing the subject, it did appear to me that the original form of the dumping clause was the more practicable one; but I must give way
to the opinions of the men who operate it and who operate under it. It was introduced some fifteen years ago. The policy that is now to be the law was introduced then; it was given a fair trial and it was found unworkable. Theory is not so powerful as the practical example and they came down to the Government and got the form recently in force enacted and they have found it workable. Those who operate under it are apparently thoroughly satisfied with it and I should think it would have been part of wisdom to leave well alone. At any rate, they claim their industry, if this clause goes into effect, will be practically ruined.
Comox-Alberni is not only a very large district, but it presents a most extraordinary diversification of interests, more so, perhaps, than any other constituency in Canada. As a matter of fact all the industries that I have mentioned are to be found and are working under a hardship in the district which I represent, and there are many other interests as well. It is for these reasons, which I will recapitulate briefly-the oriental question, the eight-hour day, the lumber industry, the coal-mining industry, the fishing industry, the dairy industry and the fruit industry -and for the reasons that I have advanced in connection with these industries, that I hesitate and wonder whether I am acting In the best interests of my constituents in supporting the Government on this occasion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I may assure my hon.
friends to my left that while I may have somewhat loose ideas and be a little wobbly on the tariff, I have an unalterable conviction that as long as I represent the constituency of Comox-Alberni, my first duty is to look after their interests and my second to look after the interests of the province from which I come. If other hon. members would do the same, we would soon be able to get together and decide on a compromise-for all legislation is compromise-that would give a reasonable regard to the interests of all the different provinces. While these things all affect that district, they are all large questions and I am not being petty or parochial in the matter. They affect, in their entirety, the whole of British Columbia; in some cases, they affect the whole of that province, in other cases, a very considerable portion of it. But they are all burning, vital questions to British Colum-
The Budget-Mr. Neill

bia as a whole. It cannot he said that these questions concerning British Columbia have not been laid before the House; all the various members from that province have spoken and at some length on these different questions. They have been backed up by representations made by boards of trade, chambers of commerce, city councils and the like, so that it cannot be said that these questions have not been presented to the Government or that the Government are in ignorance in regard to the matter. The conviction, however, has been forced on us, most unwillingly, that the country districts of British Columbia are suffering from a double injustice. In the first place, the country is being starved for the benefit of the city ridings. In the second place, British Columbia is largely a country of raw products, and the development of those raw products is largely in its initial stages. We, therefore, can justly demand in the development of those resources the same protection as was accorded Ontario and Quebec in days gone by. I do not mean only actual tariff protection; but they got assistance and protection and some of the eastern industries are getting that still. Surely, therefore, we can demand that we get the same measure of protection until we build up our industries and get upon our feet. We are, however, feeling that we are being discriminated against in favour of the more populous or more represented portions of Canada. I do not chuckle over this as my hon. friends to my right. The reason I do not chuckle is that I have to go home and explain to my constituents why I support a government which does all these things. I have striven to avoid the consummation, but I cannot disguise the facts. They are as plain to the man on the street as to any one. If this policy is persisted in I cannot see how the Government, logically or fairly, can expect a very continued support from the country members of British Columbia, or, in the case of an election, any very great accession of support from the other districts. I may be wrong, perhaps my vision is limited; but I cannot see how it can work out otherwise. During the summer it is my intention to tour my riding. I always do that during the recess, because it is the only way to keep in touch with the people and to secure a proper measure of democratic representation. Any one who desires to know what public opinion really is must keep next to the people, and I shall 
tour the districts and hold meetings, at which the public will be invited not only to listen but to talk as well. I want to hear their views and to get their sentiments; and in accordance with the views I gather there, and the judgment which the people express generally, shall my course at the next session be shaped.
Mr. FRANCIS N. McCREA (Sherbrooke) : We have been waiting for several weeks for the budget to ascertain just what our venerable Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) proposed to do in the way of taxation, and now that it has been presented it is evident that every hon. member is not satisfied. I have received letters and telegrams urging me to use my influence to persuade the minister and his colleagues to modify the budget in such respects as those who have communicated with me are affected. Personally I was inclined to be somewhat unhappy over the budget, but when I stop to realize that this country requires about half a billion dollars to meet ordinary expenses, I have not very much to say except to make up my mind, as I think every one else should, to bear my full share of taxation. Every one must be prepared to do this, and to pay a little more than he would possibly like to pay. And I have such unbounded f aith in the good judgment and the wisdom of the Minister of Finance that I am willing to leave that part to him. Consequently, I do not purpose taking up very much time discussing the pros and cons of the tariff question or of the budget. I think there is another subject of much more importance to the people than is any slight modification in the tariff here or there. That subject is our National Railway system; indeed, not only our National Railways but the other railways in the country as well. I look upon the railway situation as very serious, and the great question that is engaging the attention of the people throughout the country to-day is, what we are going to do to improve it? As a manufacturer who does a considerable amount of shipping, I find, and I think the public generally find, that the present freight rates are too high; in fact, they are so excessive that I think they are paralyzing business. Business at the present time is stagnant; it is held up to a great extent by reason of these high freight rates, for shippers cannot move their goods freely. A nd besides the freight rates being so high, the people are faced with a deficit on the government railways, of some $72,000,000,

The Budget-Mr. McCrea
as shown by the Minister of Railways; while I believe that if the minister got a proper audit and a thorough accounting we should find that the deficit is not only $72,000,000 but well over $100,000,000. If I understand the situation correctly, there has been no proper accounting made for depreciation of rolling stock, road bed, etc.; nor has there been any allowance for capital investment. I believe therefore that with a fair and proper accounting you would 4 p.m. find the deficit in the vicinity of the higher figure I have suggested. Now, there are gentlemen in this House, some of them on this side-I do not know how they come to be here, holding such views-who advocate government ownership of railways. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) the other day predicted that the time would come when we should be proud of our National Railways. Well, it is not entirely impossible that that prediction may be fulfilled some time or other. But from time immemorial there have been prophets in this world who have foretold the immediate advent- of the millennium, which is not yet here; and in my opinion the day when we shall be proud of our National Railways will be cotemporaneous with the millennium. Those of us who were in the Railway Committee room a few days ago and listened to the evidence of Mr. Beatty learned that the Canadian Pacific Railway, a private railway which is well managed, operating over practically the same territory as our National Railways, pays its stockholders something over $30,000,000 a year in the way of returns on their investments. On the other hand our nationally owned railways, operated by the Government, are creating a deficit which the people, the owners of the system, are asked to dig down into their pockets to pay. And that deficit, as I have pointed out, is around $100,000,000. The man who stands up in this House or anywhere else and seriously declares that the nationally owned railways are a good investment has more courage than judgment, in my opinion.
What are we to do in the circumstances? We have heard Mr. Beatty, the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway; we have heard Mr. Hanna, who is the chairman of Board of Directors of the National Railways; and I presume that if you asked these gentlemen who were the managers, respectively, of these corporations, they *would tell you that they were. In my
judgment neither of them manages the financial end of the road with which he is connected. I think that if you go to Indianapolis and consult Mr. Carey, the president of the international labour union, you will find that he has more to say about the financial operations of these roads than either of these gentlemen, and dictates the policy of them from the financial standpoint. To explain what I mean: A short time ago I was talking to Mr. J. H. Walsh, manager of the Quebec Central Railway, over which our company does a very large-amount of shipping. I complained of the rates, .and he said that it was true that their rates were rather exorbitant, being more than double what they were five or six years ago. "But," he said, "here is the condition of affairs. At practically every station along the line the agent's residence is in the same building in which he does his work. Ever since I have been in charge of the road, some twenty-five years now, the practice has been for one agent to look after the station, whether he worked ten or twelve hours. He was on duty in the morning, when the first train was despatched, and he was on duty m the evening to see after the last train, having put in a day of ten or twelve or perhaps thirteen hours. And he was satisfied." But under the McAdoo arrangement this method was all changed; the agents and everybody else worked on the basis of the eight-hour day. Mr. Walsh said that the agents were told: "We are willing that you should work eight hours; we do not ask you to work more. But we do ask you to spread that eight hours over the day; that is, to be on duty when the first train requires your attention in the morning. If there is no other train for two or three hours, you may do as you like during that time, but be on duty when the next train comes along and take care of it." But the reply of the men was: "We belong to the union, and they will not let us do that." The result is that these men work their eight-hour day and if a customer comes half an hour or even ten minutes late for his freight or on any other business, there is nobody to attend to him. If the work is to be done, arrangements have to be made with the agent to pay him time and a half after he has put in his eight hours. This applies to the whole system, all the way down. Mr. Walsh says that the men are being paid twice as much as they were being paid five years ago, and that it now requires two men where one man formerly
The Budget-Mr. McCrea

did the work with ease. How can you expect, he says, a reduction of freight rates under these conditions?

speechtext: I suppose they are not paid any more than other men in similar employment. But this condition applies to all railways and it is responsible for the high rates which prevail. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I say that this system applies not only to the agents but to all the railway employees. Mr. Walsh told me at the same time, by way of illustration, what now happens in the case of a locomotive which comes in for repairs. The engineer in charge runs it into the shop and reports to the master mechanic that

some repairs are necessary. The master mechanic sends a machinist to make the repairs, with all the necessary tools. But when the machinist examines the engine he finds, perhaps, that a steam pipe is leaking-possibly needs to be tightened up. Now he has all the tools, all the equipment to do that work, just as it had been done for years before this McAdoo system of running railways in Canada came into force. But he dare not touch the job; he has to send back to the shops for a steamfitter to come in and fix that pipe, though it is a job which he himself could do in five minutes. The same thing applies to half a dozen different parts of the engine. Work that one man used to do now takes three or four men before the job is completed. Now, I am not interested in the railways; I have not a dollar in railway stock. But I ship as much freight as any man in this House. I ask hon. members who criticise the railways and find fault with them: how are the railways to cope with this condition? The railways should be in a position to say to these men: "You must do thus and so, as you did before; conditions have changed; you also must change and come back to normal conditions." When a strike is called, who calls it? Mr. Carey of Indianapolis, or some other leader of an organization. In the election of 1911 we heard a great deal from our friends on the other side of the House to the effect that there should be no truck or trade with the Yankees. Well, -so far as the Yankees running our railway system is concerned; so far as their dictating when and how and how many hours our men shall work and what pay they shall receive, I say it is time that we had no truck and no trade in that direction. We ought to say: "Hands off; we will run our own business."
I am not in favour of low wages; I think I have stated that in this House before. I am a farmer's son. I was born and brought up on a farm

not a very rich one, either-and at a time when money did not come easily. Moreover, when I left my father's farm I went out as a labouring man, and without friends, without money, without anything to recommend me to the world. If I have had some degree of success it has been by putting into practice what I am now preaching to others; it has been the result of thrift and industry, of taking care of my money and not spending more than I earned. I think, therefore, I have the right to give some advice on these particular questions. I

The Budget-Mr. McCrea
say I am not in favour of very much lower wages, but I am in favour of every man, no matter what position he holds, doing an honest and fair day's work for the money he receives. This classifying of labour- and there are some men in this House who know the results of it-this classifying of labour which calls upon a man to do a particular work and forbids him to do anything else, has cost this country a lot of money. I have no quarrel with labour; what I am saying now is, I believe, in the best interests of labour. I say to the young man in this country who is starting out as I did, without friends, relations, education or anything else to recommend him, the best thing he can do is to show his employer that he is interested in his work and trying to earn money for him. That ,is the way he will get promotion. If his employer does not notice his faithfulness and other good qualities, somebody else will. That is the best road to success that I know of.
Mr. Beatty, in his evidence before the Railway Committee the other day, said that he proposed to reduce the rates, but he was very cautious to add1, on conditions, and what were the conditions? On condition that labour costs were reduced. If Mr. Beatty and Mr. Hanna were the managers of these two great railway systems as they ought to be, they would be able to say: "We are going to reduce the rates." But they are only in a position to say: "We will reduce the rates if Mr. Carey allows us, and if he does not, we cannot help ourselves." I do not know whether everybody in this House realizes it or not, but in my judgment our railway rates have reached such an exorbitant point that business is practically paralyzed, and on top of that we have $100,000,000 of deficits on the government-owned1 railways. I ask the Government and this House what are we going to do to remedy the situation? During the war, prices of everything went up, materials, wheat, lumber and everything else. Railway rates also went up; that was all right, and so did wages. Now we have reached the period where the prices of all commodities have diminished, in some cases more than 50 per cent, but labour costs have not come down in proportion. What we ask, and what we have the right to ask, of labour is that their costs should come down in proportion to the value of the goods they produce, but they do not appear to be willing to allow that. I say that if this Government have the power to legislate on the question, they should do so, and if they have not the power, we should hold a conference as they did in England, to see what they will allow us to do, because the situation is so grave. To my mind these are the only two courses, and one of them we cannot adopt too soon. If we have the power to say to these people: "You shall not go on strike," or "You shall not hold up the business of this country"

whichever way you choose to put it-if we have that power, all right. If we have not, let us invite them to a conference, take off our hats, and say: "Gentlemen, what will you allow us to do? The conditions are so grave that we cannot go on this way much longer, and some remedy must be found." I am not complaining about wages so much as the lack of efficiency. Labour is clamouring for shorter hours and more pay. I do not object so much to the more pay as I do to the Shorter hours. There is a strike of the coal miners on in the United States at the present time, and one of their demands is for a six-hour day-the six hours to be counted from the time they leave the surface until they get back up again-and a five-day week. How can we expect cheap transportation when the steam for hauling our freight has to be generated from coal mined under those conditions? What right has a man who has to work for a living, whether he be a coal miner or any body else, to ask that the industry he is engaged in shall receive such a price for its products that it can afford to employ him for a six-hour day and a five-day week, or thirty hours a week altogether, when the farmer and the man who feeds that labouring man has to work seven days a week and anywhere from ten to fifteen hours a day?
Here is the situation. The people of this country are made up of groups. They do not all work in the same shop. One group is making boots and shoes, another group clothing, another group hats and caps, and so on. But there is another group, which comprises at least fifty per cent of the total population of Canada, and it is those who till the soil, and that group cannot carry on their business on an eight-hour day or a forty-four hour week. I am speaking now of the dairy farmer, not the wheat miner as some people call him; he can probably get along on shorter hours; but the dairy farmer who produces the butter, the cheese, the eggs, the beef, the pork, the mutton, the vegetables, and all the rest that goes to feed the nation, has to work six days a week and do his chores on Sunday, and he is very lucky if he gets the chance to go to church. The dairy farmer is not the only one who has to work long hours. It is the

The Budget

Mr. McCrea
same in the lumbering industry. You cannot river-drive or carry on lumbering operations on a six-hour day. And there are many other industries in that category. I ask, what right has the man who works in a shoe factory and makes the shoes the farmer has to buy to say that the farmer must pay sufficient money for those shoes to enable that factory to pay its labour on the basis of an eight-hour day or a forty-four hour week, when the farmer himself is working six days a week and anywhere from ten to fifteen hours a day? "Someone may say that the farmer is idling part of his time, that he does net work on rainy days, for instance. I was brought up on the farm, and I know there are all kinds of farmers, as well as all kinds of labourers. There are labourers who will not work until starvation forces them, and farmers who work when they must, but these are not the ones who contribute to the feeding of the nation. I am speaking of the men who feed the nation, the men who work six days a week, and have to do their chores on Sunday, or get somebody else to do them, and who are lucky if they can go to church. What right has the man who produces the coal, or the boots, or the clothing, to say to the farmer: "You must work ten or twelve hours a day, or longer, in order to produce what I require at low prices, while I on my side will work only forty-four hours a week, and loaf most of that time if I can"? I have lived a long time, but I have yet to learn where honest, faithful toil has ever killed anybody. I believe in honest, faithful toil, and in prudence and economy, and if you want to succeed that is my rule of success.
Some people may say: If you work every man ten hours a day, and every man works to his capacity, there will not be work enough to go round, and a lot of people will in consequence be idle. That may be true of China or any densely populated country, but in this young Canada of ours, with a population of less than ten million and a capacity to accommodate one hundred and fifty millions of people, with millions of acres of untilled, first-class choice land as good as any in the world, with her inexhaustible mineral and forest wealth,

does any man tell me that there is not enough work in this country for everybody who is willing to work? We are told today that there are numbers of men in the large cities out of employment

speechtext:
-and I wish to say further: that the great majority of the men that are walking the streets and claiming they are in search of work are looking for positions, not work; positions where they can get a living with practically nothing to do. There are always lots of men engaged in that kind of quest. At the same time, it is true that we are passing through extremely hard times, and I say that if there are men or women that are destitute and are willing to work but cannot get

The Budget-Mr. McCrea
employment, and have no money upon which to subsist, the country should take care of them. Nevertheless such people should be told "This country has resources and employment can be found for every man and every woman who is able and willing to work We are going to help you now but see to it that you do not fall into need again. Take care of yourself; find some employment because there is plenty for you to do." If there are so many idle people why have we an immigration policy seeking to bring outsiders to this country? Either we have room and employment for immigrants, or conditions are such that we do not want any more outsiders.
I have a remedy for the existing situation and I am going to explain it to the House, but I would not advise this or any other government to adopt the suggestion right off. Let them ponder it well and if they think as I do they will come to the conclusion that the remedy is one worth trying. But the people will need to be educated to an understanding of what the proposition means, and of the beneficial results which will follow. My proposition is this: In the first place I would say to the labouring class, or any other class, that if they wish to form a union they have a perfect right to do that, because in union there is strength. But if they form a union they should do it under the laws of the country in the same manner that any other incorporated company is formed- if any company wishes to commence operations in Canada the first thing it must do is get a charter. That charter defines what the company may or may not do, and sets forth that those concerned are amenable to the law and must live up to any agreement into which it enters. I maintain that the first thing the government ought to do is to pass a law that a union of labour men, or organization of any other kind, must be responsible and amenable to the laws of the land. The next step should be to select from among the best men available persons learned in the law and persons experienced in industrial, labour, and other matters, to form a board to deal with labour situations. Then the government should make it an unlawful offence either for employees to walk out or for employers to declare a lock-out. That does not mean that capital and labour would not be always able to agree when differences arose, but what would happen would be this: In the event of a failure on the part of the representatives of labour to agree with the representatives of the
particular company concerned, both sides should go before this commission and be heard as in the case of proceedings in a court of justice. After hearing the facts the commission would give its finding, which would be binding on both parties to the dispute. In the meantime there would have been no strike, and no holding up of business. At present, men go on strike because they have no other remedy-that is the only course open to them. Why not try an arbitration first, why not try to reach a settlement before deciding to stike? It is not merely the men and their employers that are interested; the public generally are concerned. For example, take the strike which occurred in New York last fall when probably three or four thousand milk drivers, and a number of milk dealers went out. What was the outcome? There was almost an epidemic among thousands of children in New York, where they were depending on getting milk and could not get it. Why should such a thing exist? Is that a humane way to settle trouble? I claim it is not.
The nations engaged in the great war which ended a few years ago lost millions of men, and after the war they met in order to settle terms of peace, which are not settled yet. Why should they not have had this agreement before? We should have a period of education, and people should be taught the proper way to settle such matters. I think seventy-five to ninety per cent of the men who go on strike cannot afford to do it, and fifty per cent do not want to strike. The men who make a business of engineering these strikes go round, hold meetings, and make the men believe that their employers are the greatest enemies they have, and are trying to crush and ruin them, when the facts are exactly the opposite. Any employer of labour who understands his business-and I think most of them do-realize that the goodwill of their employees is the best asset they can have, and they have no desire to crush those employees. The commission which I propose would deal with that aspect of it, and would do justice to all parties. The reason I suggest a period of education in these matters is because the men have only heard one side of the story. They have listened to the agitators, who tell them their employers are trying to crush theta out of existence. Under the arrangement I propose, men will have their differences settled by the commission, and will receive their just and honest dues. The commissioners will be men of experience and the
The Budget-Mr. McCrea

matter will Ibe settled in the interests of the men and everybody concerned. Under these conditions, the employer could afford to pay his men better money. At present, if a contract of some magnitude is to be let in this city or elsewhere, the man who proposes to tender for that contract does not know where he is at. Suppose he tenders, is awarded the contract, and gets everything ready, and the labourers ask wages that he cannot conceive to be reasonable. Then they go oni strike, and months elapse, and perhaps the period during which the work should be d'one will have passed. The consequence may be that the contractor is called upon to do the work in the fall or winter, when it would 'cost double the money it would cost at another period. The contractor does not make any money, and the labourers do not make any money because they are on strike. Under the system of arbitration, if the labourers did not agree with the contractor who tendered for a certain work, he would know there would be no strike on his hands. But he might have to pay the men more money, but that would be a mere bagatelle compared with the cost of doing the work at the wrong time of the year, when it cannot be done to advantage.

speechtext:
The labour Clement of the country has only heard the agitator's end of the story, and he would be out of a job if my plan were1 put into effect, but that would be a benefit to all concerned. I come from the city of Sherbrooke, and two-thirds of my electors, at least, belong to the labouring class. I have expressed my views to them before, and I am not afraid to do it again. In my opinion1 it is the solution of this trouble, and I believe when this Government goes before the country again they would be well advised if they adopted my suggestion or something along similar lines. I believe it is reasonable, fair and just to all parties. Can any hon. member show me a case where, being dissatisfied with their Conditions, men have _ gone out on strike for one week or six months, and have derived any benefit? In cases of strikes, finally, after having exhausted what little means they have, the men come down to a method of adjustment. Why not have the adjustment before the strike, instead of after? I believe it is proper for the men to form unions to put

their case 'before the public; but if they are going to unionize the men should do it under the law of the country and should1 not be allowed to do it in any other way. Under present conditions when a strike takes place a commission is appointed to investigate. Nine times out of ten the members of that commission have had no experience in regard to labour or capital. The commissioner may be a judge, perhaps learned in the law, but he knows nothing about labour. I propose to have men of experience in this particular work, who know what is necessary and what is fair and just to both parties. The troubles between the men and the employers could be adjusted, with no tie-up of business conditions. In cases of strikes it is not merely the labourers and employers who are affected, but, in Cases of railway strikes, the whole community suffers. I contend that the very best asset any man can have in the industrial world is the goodwill of his employees. If he has not that, I pity him. I have been a labourer; I have been an employer of labour for many years, and the best asset I want to have, or believe I can have, is to have the goodwill and good wishes of the men who work for me. I have, however, never yet allowed, and I do not intend to allow any man to dictate to me and say: "This is my particular job; I will do this and I will do nothing else; I am hired to do this work, and if I can do it in an hour a day, I will not do anything else." If a man agrees to work for me eight hours a day and I agree to pay him for that, I expect him to work for me eight hours a day; and if there is something which he can do in the interest of me or the company which I represent, I expect him to do it. Surely that is a reasonable request. So long as the railways in this country are run on the McAdoo system of every man having a particular work which is classified, and is not being permitted to do anything else, we need not look for cheaper rates or better conditions. The sooner we get away from the idea that every man should have a fixed job and nothing else, the better it will be for everybody.
I think I have taken up enough of the time of the House; but I wish to touch upon one other matter. In the Agricultural Committee a few days ago I made some remarks which evidently pleased some people and displeased others. The only comment I care to make upon the matter is that, as my remarks were made in the committee they are not published in

The Budget-Mr. McCrea
Hansard, and the only report is the report made by the newspapers. In that particular case, the report of part of what I said was correct, but part of my remarks was omitted. I commenced my remarks with regard to the Civil Service by saying that, in the Civil Service, there were a number of good men and good women who were earning the money they were getting and who were capable of earning more provided they worked more hours, as I think they should. I also said that quite a number of them were not earning their money. In addition to that I think I said-I do not want my remarks to be interpreted as meaning that these people were no good-that when you employ more men than you have work for, people who have not anything to do become parasites. I said that in the Civil Service there were a certain number of employees who were simply parasites because they were not earning their money, and the reason that they were not earning their money was because they had not sufficient work to do, as the service was overmanned. That was my statement, and I do not propose to retract it, whether it pleases or displeases. I also said that my advice to the Government would be as soon as possible to get busy and dispense with the services of those whom they did not require. I also said that many of these people were Overpaid and that they were not earning their money. I have had some comment from different parties; I heard very loud talk of their poverty, how they were underpaid and badly treated, how they were living in almost starvation conditions. All I have to say in that respect is this: If anybody doubts that they are pretty prosperous people, let him walk down the streets about this time -it is now about a quarter to five, and they are not supposed to be out until five o'clock; but you will find many of them a little ahead of time-and you will think they are coming out of church. Just notice how they are dressed. If you saw the two crowds, one coming out of the government offices and the other coming from church, you would not know which was which.
I should like to cite some figures. I have always been in favour of giving good wages to people who earn their money, and I have no objection to paying good wages to the Civil Service or any other service, because my judgment is that that is the only way to deal with workers who earn their money. But when civil servants complain about
their meagre salaries or wages, we must consider that their hours of labour are six and a half hours a day. Those are supposed to be the hours of labour, but they do not always work that number of hours. Take for instance, a man or a woman receiving $1,000 a year for 300 days a year and six and a half hours a day, you will find that he or she gets 51J cents an hour for every hour's service that he or she is supposed to put in. Any person who wants to hire labour can hire as much as he wants and can get it to work hard for much less than that. The man who receives $1,200 a year is being paid at the rate of 61 cents an hour; the man who receives $1,400 a year is being paid at the rate of 73 cents an hour. The man who receives $2,000 a year is getting $1.03 for every hour he works, and the man who gets $2,400 a year receives $1.23 for every hour he works. My contention is: If they are not satisfied with the money they are receiving, in the first place, why did they take the job? In the second place, why do they not get something else to do somewhere else? Conditions are such to-day that everybody is asked to retrench and cut down expenses, and iit is no more hardship on the Civil Service than on anybody else to cut down expenses and live within their means, especially at the present time when, as an hon. member said, many men are walking the streets and cannot get anything to do at all. Two or three years ago, conditions may have been somewhat different; but today we have reached a point that when you walk into a saloon and call for a drink of lemonade, you are taxed a few cents additional to pay for the cost of running the country and the deficit on the government-owned railways. Every cheque you sign has to have an extra stamp or two .put on it for the same reason. Surely, then, it is time for the people to consider which way we are travelling and to economize. Whether the Civil Service are pleased or displeased, we should say to them: "If you are not satisfied with conditions, the best thing for you to do is to economize, and if you are still not satisfied, you can go and find work somewhere else."

make a statement? The ihon. gentleman has repeated two or three times that I am opposed to organized labour. I said that I am not opposed; that I thought it was necessary that labour should be organized. I am not opposed to organized labour, but I am opposed to its running the country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is all very well for the hon. member now to say that he is in favour of organized labour.' But was there ever such a denunciation of the right of labour to organize in this country &3 has come from him to-day? My hon. friend is a pulp manufacturer, and in connection with the industry in which he is interested he recognizes the principle of

collective bargaining. In his business that principle is observed every day. The trouble in Canada to-day, however, is not so much that we have organized labour, or that we are perplexed over public ownership, as it is in the fact that there has been a lot of profiteering as a result of the war. Pex-haps the charge will apply to organized labour to some extent, but it no doubt applies to the industries of the country and the capitalists behind them; and if that is the case my hon. friend is narrow in his denunciation of organized labour. He must take a broad view of things and' recognize the right of labour to organize, as that right is recognized the world over. No doubt mistakes have been made and unfair things done under the aegis of organized labour; but I say there was never such profiteering, as a result of the war, as was practised in connection with organized industries of the character and organization which my hon. friend represents. Just think of what the pulp manufacturers did to the banks of the country, and, through them, to the people. They wrecked more homes in Montreal through speculation in paper stocks, and so forth, than anything else in the country did; and the thing is still going on. I know one bank in the country that lost $6,000,000 to one of these pulp organizations. And I know what I lost myself, because the paper makers with whom I had been doing business for thirty or forty years actually told me, after I had paid them millions of dollars: "We don't want your business any longer; take it away and close your accounts." And when the accounts were closed they had to give me back a cheque. Why should an ordinary publisher in this country be told, by men with whom he had been doing business for nearly forty years, that his business was no longer wanted and that he could take it away? I know how that treatment originated. But it has been the experience, of nearly everyone in the country that there has been profiteering on an enormous scale on the part of men carrying on industries, just as there may have been something of the kind in connection with labour. The hon. gentleman not only denounced the late government and its policy, but he eulogized the farmers, saying what a fine lot they were and how hard they worked. Well, they number 65 strong in this House, and they are here as an organized body. They have a right to organize and come here as collective bargainers, and surely they will not deny the same right to labour.
