speechtext:
My hon. friend will be able to speak for himself later. I say that the greatest strike in the world to-day is being put up by the farmers' bloc in the United States Congress, and an approach is being made to the same thing m this country. My hon. friends have my sympathy, I admit, because the farmer in Canada, no doubt, has some grievances. And the hon. member opposite (Mr. Mc-Crea) evidently does not want to allow them any relief in connection with the railways. His argument was not quite logical to me, and he did not state the full facts. However, I shall come to that in due course. Now, at a time when we are trying to pull the railways out of the difficulties in which they are struggling today, my hon. friend wants the Government to assume the responsibility of calling a halt and adopting the strange policy of going to the schoolhouses with a certain propaganda of instruction to the farmers as to how they should, or rather should not, organize, continuing that course of education for a time, and then appointing some board of arbitration to pass certain regulations with the object of denying the right of collective bargaining. If his remarks mean anything they simply mean that we should pass laws to put men into gaol- I believe those are among the words he used-if they refuse to accept certain decisions that may be given on labour matters. In the twentieth century he is preaching a doctrine centuries old, a doctrine the practice of which has caused untold mischief in the history of the world. Among those people who are gradually being freed from the conditions that have held them down for centuries is the ordin-
5 p.m. ary agricultural labourer in England. We hear a great deal about the beauty of England and how splendid a place it is in so many respects. But the other side of the story is not so engaging, especially when we remember that there are so many agricultural labourers lying in the village churchyards in that country without any headstones to tell who
they are. England was made great by economic injustice to the labouring population, not only to those who work in factories but those who labour on the farms as well; and the only hope which the labouring classes of Britain and of Europe, who have suffered this injustice for over two hundred years, have of improving their situation is by some form of collective bargaining, or unionism.
My hon. friend denounced the railways of the country, but he suppresses the main facts. He says that there is an awful situation in connection with the railways to-day. So there is. But who brought it about? The politicians, among whom are he and I. It is the orgy of railway expenditures which have been voted during the past twenty years that has brought about this condition and helped to demoralize transportation, until the governments of this country, but particularly the last government, decided that there should be no more subsidizing of railways. And, inasmuch as the railways were bankrupt, it was deemed wise to take them over and consolidate them. Now we have the roads and we are faced with a deficit, and the way to decrease that deficit is first of all to coordinate all the railways that we have now on our hands. When will the policy be brought forward which the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) promised us in the statement he submitted to Parliament some time ago? He told us that we were to have a high-class board to administer the roads and that economies would be effected by the consolidation of the three or four systems that we have. When we can do that we can hope to be able to make a decent showing. But it is because certain railways are opposed to public ownership, fearing the competition from that source, that the effort is being made now to thwart the consolidation of the National Railways and the putting of a proper business administration at their head. Now, that criticism does not apply to the Government; it would be an unfair criticism of the Government, and I do not think that any one *would resent it more than the Prime Minister, the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Labour. The railway men have possibly made mistakes; and the McAdoo award may have been wrong. There have been many mistakes made in this world in connection with other organizations, and undoubtedly mistakes may have been made by the railways. But what has been done has been done, and we must deal with the situation as it exists and take steps

2324	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. W. F. Maclean
to remedy it. But you cannot remedy it by such means as my hon. friend proposes. He makes a proposition for the suppression of strikes; but he can suppress strikes only by keeping an organized police force of 100,000 men at a great expense to the country. I think the hon. gentleman was rather juvenile in his discussion of the question, as well as in his reasoning. We must face the condition of affairs which exists. A number of our working people have but one trade; the character of our industrial organization may have brought that about. Of course, the ideal condition is that under which a man has his little farm, his little home, an acre of land1 and a cow. But the world of to-day is not organized in that way, nor are we to be relieved from the awful effects of the late war by any such condition. We must have organization, of capital, of labour, of industry. Why, even the political parties in this country are based on organization; the only thing is-and I want to tell it to my friends opposite-the two old parties think that nobody else has the right to organize and get into the same business. The arguments my hon. friend has made may be interesting talk for the day; it may suit his constituents; he may be able to say these things to the working people in his own home town. But he is not living in this century; he is not facing isquarely the problems which are confronting the people of Canada. For my part, I propose to address myself to the actual questions which face us and to which it is my right in a debate like this to direct the attention of the House.
One of the outstanding results of the war and of the Imperial conferences that have been held has relation to the status of Canada. At one time we were simply a Crown colony, but our status has expanded; greater responsibilities have come to us, and I see nothing ahead of us but a reconsideration of the whole question as to where we are and in what direction we are going constitutionally. As hon. gentlemen know, the British Empire is bound together by the principle of loyalty to the Crown. The supremacy of the Crown rests upon an act of Parliament, and that act of Parliament, which regulates the royal succession of the House of Brunswick, may be repealed any day by a democratic revolution in the form of a general election in England. If our position in the Empire is subject to that state of affairs, we must begin to think of what is 
going to happen. In view of the recognition of the dominions as co-equal with the Mother Country, it seems to me that we are coming to a condition where there will have to be some kind of federation of all these dominions on the basis of a written instrument. Strange to say, the whole policy of the British communities is not the result of a written instrument, as in the case of the United States; it is based on acts of the British Parliament which can be repealed at any time. I say that there will have to be a federation of English-speaking communities, especially those which enjoy British institutions; and under the written instrument on which it is based the various states will have the right to make their own constitutions. I stand here to-day in favour of Canada having the absolute authority to make her own constitution, just as the Commonwealth of Australia has done. That will come in a very short time, and we must prepare ourselves for it. In fact it is being forced upon us as the result of the war and of the Imperial conferences to which I have referred. Particularly in view of the uncertainty as to what war is to be in the future, this greater federation will have to deal with the question of what powers shall be granted to these free states which compose it. We shall get as a result of that not only the right to make our own constitution, but the right to establish our own courts and to have a court of last resort under Canadian law. Not for one moment do I say that Canada will ever achieve what we have always said she should achieve if the present condition in that respect continues. I believe there will have to be a supreme court of some kind as between the members of the league, or federation, whatever you like to call it; but so far as Canada is concerned, I agree with what has been said in this House and out of it, that these matters should be placed under Canadian law and be determined in Canadian courts by Canadian judges, who shall hear the arguments of Canadian lawyers, and the decisions ought to be filed in this country, no matter what they concern. While it is otherwise, we are more or less in a state of tutelage.
The most interesting question which now confronts us in this respect is with regard to war. War has not ceased. The great chemists, the greatest men of science, are busy to-day devising the most devilish systems for the destruction of humanity, and we are fools if we do not pay some

The Budget-Mr. W. F. Maclean
attention to the question of what we ought to do in the matter of defence. I see no way out of it but an early convention of the different parts of the British Empire which will comprise this league of states to which I have referred, and this convention will have to decide what we are to do in the matter of war. We must settle the question whether this damnable system of scientific destruction of humanity is to be allowed to have a free hand from now on. That is the danger to every community. The time, unfortunately, has come when a peaceful country cannot for a moment maintain its place when such a war comes on unless it is ready for it. And some war of that kind is right ahead of us. Germany may be preparing for war; she has some of the ablest scientific men in the world. Some things were disclosed during the late war which indicated in an astounding way the extent to which human destruction could be carried on. Ships were destroyed from aeroplanes by radio control of bombs, and I want to tell the House that inventions of that kind have been and are now being worked out, and humanity is up against them for the future. It is time we had a convention of this kind and that we decided what we shall do in the way of our defence. True, we can hope for what arbitration may bring about. We have a League of Nations with its seat at The Hague, to which international questions are referred, and an effort is being made to get all the nations to agree to do away with war, but they have not done it so far. It is true they are scrapping certain ships and cutting down expenditure on armament, but some kind of war is ahead of us. Some kind of great constitutional shake-up is also ahead of us, as one of the nations under the British Crown. These questions must be considered; much as we dislike to talk about them, they are ahead of us, and we cannot evade them. We have to come to a decision as to what our position shall be in the British Empire, and also on the consequent question, what are to be our rights and duties in connection with our constitution:-Are we to be absolutely free within our own country? Such questions must come up and must all be decided. It is the result of our constitutional growth and development. We may have to come to a decision pretty soon on the question of defence. We are certainly up against it financially, as this budget shows. Enormous sums of money have to be raised, and heavy taxation is 148i
being imposed. With this taxation ahead of us, it is time that we began to consider and discuss these questions in a broad way.
Another question that is coming up is that of race aggression. We have to protect our own races in this country. We are threatened by all kinds of racial aggression to-day, and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) dealt with that subject for a moment. There is an attempt on the part of the orientals, and on the part of people in eastern and south eastern Europe, to get a foothold in this country. We must consider whether the races in this country can keep their position and endure in view of this inrush of orientals and Europeans I have before me a telegram in connection with that immigration from Europe, which I shall read a little later on. It is another question on which we must come to some kind of a decision.
Now I come to the question of transportation, and other associated questions raised by my hon. friend, and I want to bring them up in a rather broad way. We have had these questions discussed in this House and all over this country. I am going to lay down here to-day, and I ask the attention of hon. gentlemen to it, a Bill of Eights for the public services of this country. I have been studying this matter very carefully for the last two weeks and I have put the issue in shape for presentation to-day to the House and the country. Now what is this Bill of Rights that is hastening on in this country so fast that we cannot quite appreciate it? Let me read it to the House, and I invite the attention of hon. gentlemen who care to say something about it. I intend to make this Bill of Rights a part of my speech, and it will be printed in Hansard to-morrow:
Bill of Rights of Canadian Public Services.
The Government of Canada by itself or in association with others, or by delegation to others, to acquire, undertake and operate the following public services:
1.	Transportation:	A National System of
Transportation, in and out of Canada, by railway, highway, waterway, airway or other way or means, singly or jointly, including warehouses, elevators, terminal facilities, and also including the purchase, production, distribution and sale of electrical or other energy or source thereof.
2.	Communications: A National System of Communications in and out of Canada by post, express, wire, wave or other means, singly or jointly.
3.	Banking: A National System of Banking in and out of Canada associated with the Post Office or banks or bankers or otherwise, including rediscounting for banks and provinces,
2326	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. W. F. Maclean
the making of advances on warehouse receipt or other security.
4.	Marketing: A National System of Marketing of farm and other staple products, with or without co-operation of organized producers or holders thereof, including the making of advances on such products in store or other security until marketed.
5.	Waterways for sea vessels: The Government of Canada by itself or in conjunction with the United States or others to establish waterways for sea-going vessels to Inland lake and river ports: and wherever possible to develop water or other power for the movement of traffic as may be agreed upon.
Finance: Such services to be financed out of the National Treasury, or by arrangements with banks or others or by bond issue of the national government or of others, bearing bank or bond interest, further secured when so provided on the undertaking or product.
Management:	The administration of any
such national service or any other public service in whole or in part, may be associated with that of any other public service in whole or in part; And these or other public services, wherever possible, to be made community centres so as to secure day and night service and every day service and efficient service to the greatest number of beneficiaries thereof or participants therein.
That, I take it, is a Bill of Rights in regard to these public services, and every one of the principles involved therein has been adopted more or less by this House, but they have never been brought together in this way. I have put them together in this form, and I take the responsibility of saying that on this Bill of Rights the next general election in Canada will be fought. It deals with transportation, with communications, with banking, with marketing, with waterways for sea vessels, and the financing and management of these services. As I said, all these matters have come up in this House, but they have all been disassociated from one another. The time has come when there can be no more trifling in this House with these services; we must deal with them adequately, or throw them out. We must either have, or not have, a national system of transportation. If we are to have a national system of transportation, it must be broad enough to take in every means of transport mentioned in this Bill of Rights. It must included the railway, the highway, the radial, the boat on the lake and on the sea. We have been told in the past in this House that there could be no regulation of freight rates in this country because some freight passes by boats, and boats were not under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. I am not aware if the hon. members of this House know what hard work some of us had to get even vessels carrying the traffic of this country brought under the

Railway Act. We did succeed in that, and now we are proposing develcpments in other directions. For example, there are what the French call "communications", embracing the post office, express, telegraph and telephone services. We are conducting all these to-day, but the work should be done on well defined grounds and under well defined responsibility. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. MacT-aren) had a question on the Order Paper to-day dealing with the matter of cables. We have got immense investments in cables that we hardly know of; we also have immense investments in telegraphs, and similar investments in the wireless system. All these services we must co-ordinate and consolidate, and not turn them over to a private company as has been done in the States. The greatest monopoly in the world to-day is not the Standard Oil Company; it is the telegraph and telephone combination which has jits headquarters in Boston and is taking over all the British cables. How many of us know that, except a few members who are interested in that subject? The same combination have taken over all the land lines in the States, and most of the other associated interests. That combination is the American Telegraph and Telephone Company; it is not the Westing-house Company. The commitments in Canada, to which I have alluded, are so great, the services are so great, that, in these progressive times, now that they have got into the hands of the state and are being handled by the state, they must be co-ordinated. Furthermore we must have community centres in which these services will play an important part, as I pointed out in the declaration which I read. Why should not the post office, and the government telegraph, express and money order business, be located in a little central office in a community centre? That is what the West wants to-day more than anything else. Now ;that we are having public ownership of railways I hope we shall also have in the West, in every hamlet and every township, some kind of a community centre controlled by the government and that government handling the post office, the telegraph service and the express service, all adjacent to the telephone system, having an all-night and an all-day service such as the people want. But we cannot carry on business efficiently in the future unless we co-ordinate all these services; and, as I said before, there is not one of these

The Budget-Mr. W. F. Maclean
things we have not already done in this country only it was in a disconnected way.
The right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) who led the late government, and his associates, engaged in a banking business in this country and they helped to save Canada. It is considered to be a disgrace that the country shall be in the banking business; but during the war we carried on a system of re-discounting for the banks the facts as to which have never been disclosed to the people. There is no reason why the credit of the nation should not be used to a reasonable degree in connection with the marketing of our farm products, and other similar lines, but we ought to declare where we stand on these questions.
Now I come to one more thought on the subject of the employment of our waterways for seagoing vessels. The President of the United States-as far as we could gather from the public press, and from what the Prime Minister of Canada said here the other day-has made certain proposals to this Government in connection with the St. Lawrence waterways. Well, the Progressive element in the United States, the farmer's bloc, are in favour of the scheme. They are insisting on it, and it is their force which has compelled action by the United States government. The farmers to-day are the most dominating party in the United States; they have more influence in the American Senate than any other party, and they are compelling action by the so-called old fashioned Senate; they are the most progressive parliamentary party to be found over there. They have discussed all these questions which affect the farmers, including the transportation question, and while the stage of public ownership of transportation has not yet been reached they have come to approve of public ownership of the waterways and the development of electrical energy along those waterways for the traffic of the country. That is coming in the United States, and why should we not be willing to co-operate with that country in developing the St. Lawrence waterways? The Canadian government may have some reason why the question should not come up just now, but I hope they are not influenced in their action by the eastern seaports and the eastern cities of Canada. Because those seaports and those interests are assuming a dictatorial policy as to conduct and action, and as to what the people of the West should do in regard to their transportation problems. They have denied to us the right of free access to their ports
and to their services for ocean going vessels carrying western products, and there is actually an organization in Canada now, and especially the city of Montreal and particularly in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway, seeking to declare that we shall not have this development in connection with the Northwest and that we shall not have the benefit of sea transportation. What is the secret of the success of the cities and towns of Europe today? Is it due to the railroads? Over there seaports are open all the year round, and ships can navigate rivers and go from one inland place to another. Europe today is absolutely served and protected by a system of navigation, by freedom and interchange in the use of the sea, in the use of the railways, and in the use of the highways. In that way they are working out a great improvement in commerce. In this country to-day an organization is being perfected, and it has its headquarters in connection with the railroads of this country, having for its object to see to it that there shall not be waterway competition with the railways. The whole hope of the Canadian West is in getting water transportation, and reduced freight rates from that source alone. There has been more reduction effected in the cost of transportation by water competition than by anything else; but the railway interests to which I have referred do not like to see that competition and there is an organization entrenched in Montreal, perhaps in the Maritime provinces, perhaps somewhere in the city of Quebec, that would deny every port on lake Ontario, every port on lake Erie, every port on lake Huron, and every port on lake Superior its right to sea waterways and to the improvement of traffic charges. It is the most domineering system we have ever had in Canada. It is even said they are holding up the Prime Minister in regard to any policy he may have contemplated in connection with this matter. Well, when the issue as to this Bill of Rights is fought out I imagine the people will compel decisive action of some sort. I imagine that when the next election is fought it will be on these questions of transportation, communications, marketing, and banking. As I have already said, we have nibbled at every one of these issues. I do not know whether hon. gentlemen opposite, when they were previously in office, were committed to any of them or not. To-day we have national railways and national telegraphs, and we have to go the

The Budget-Mr. W. F. Maclean
whole hog or none. We have some national banking. The greatest system of banking in the world to-day is the national banking system of United 'States, behind1 which they have the credit of the United1 States government, and to-day the United States is the master of finance for the world. She is coming to the relief of all countries. She has, time after time, come to the relief of the cotton growers and wheat growers of the United States. Mr. McAdbo has1 been very much denounced by the previous speaker. Well do I remember the time when the cotton and wheat men could not get money from the bankers-, or had to pay 8, 9 or 10 per cent for it, and Mr. McAdoo, secretary of the treasury, said "Farmers you will get all the money you want for the movement of your crop in the shape of credit and government notes of the United1 States"-and the farmers were able to move their crops.

There is a good deal in that argument, and some very good immigrants have come to this country from portions of Europe. We must, however, have, in connection with immigration, a policy that first of all will protect the races which are already in this country, and we cannot he quite swamped by the people of Russia or the orientals from the East. We want our country settled, and we want farmers from every country in the world to come here if they wish to do so. We desire a broad immi-' gration policy; but the people whom we want most of all are farmers who will toil on the land. Very good farmers have come to this country from Russia and from southeastern Europe. It is important that the Government should adopt and shortly put into force some national policy of immigration; but we must consider the people who are here to-day, who have to carry on in this country and who do not wish to see it come quite into the hands of other races. In portions of the United States to-day, the American population is outnumbered by the foreign population, and, perhaps, a similar condition is coming to us in connection with orientals. Nobody likes to hear of the invasion of our country by the Japanese as a nation, their lumbermen taking up our Crown lands, oriental labour being brought in by gangs and paid by the Japanese government, and not a particle of that work going to Canadian workers. It rather makes one blush to think that a nation, with which we have been very friendly in the war and which we have helped a great deal, is actually going to take possession of our forests, to bring its nationals into our country to do the lumbering and to export that lumber, and to do this as a national proposition of Japan. That will hardly go down with Canadians, but it is a question which Parliament must deal with in very short order.
While I have, perhaps, trespassed upon the time of the House in bringing up these questions, I have tried to deal with them not from any party standpoint. They are vital questions which confront us, and what I have laid down to-day is a bill of rights in connection with the public services of Canada. That is going to be the issue in the next election; and to get 
ready for that election, hon. gentlemen in charge of the government to-day must prepare for redistribution in this country and give full representation. If they do not do that this session, they will have to do it next session.

I do not know how I am going to come out of the scrimmage; but I am going to tell the people that, no matter what I have been in the past, I am in favour of that bill of rights before anything else in the public services of this country. Progressive ideas are now affecting the people and they are talking and reading about what questions will be discussed in the coming election. These things are treated in that bill of rights, and I want my hon. friends from the West to read it over and when they take the floor to be good enough to tell this House and the country whether there is anything in that bill of rights in regard to all these public questions. If there is I am satisfied to have those questions go to the people.
The old political traditions that have obtained in this country have now come to an end. At present we are in a bog, largely because of the war and as a result of our own political action and legislation in the past. But if wre are to get on to solid ground again, we must pull ourselves together, cease to be partisans to the extent that we have been in the past, and instead, be first of all Canadians, with a faith in the future of our country. Let us make our constitution and our courts supreme; let us so act that we shall play a worthy part in the League of Nations of which, with Australia, South Africa, and the rest of the Empire, we form an important part. Parliamentary government to-day is the best institution in the world. We have inherited that form of government from the Mother Country, which has done more for the world than any other nation; and parliamentary government is based upon the principle that the voice of the people shall be expressed and crystallized in progressive legislation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not fully persuaded in my own mind that I have a contribution worthy of this moment or of the subject in the discussion of which we are engaged. I feel it incumbent upon me, however, to define my attitude very briefly and very succinctly on these proposals that have been submitted to us by the hon. Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) in his annual budget.
The great task confronting the people of Canada in this crisis-a task, of course, that confronts a finance minister in a very direct and distinct sense-is the task of meeting our financial obligations, and meeting them by methods that will bring the utmost measure of relief to what we ordinarily designate as agriculture on the one hand and the great masses of Canadian workmen on the other. When I say "the utmost measure of relief", I have in my mind such relief as is compatible with national stability and national progress. The position-shall I say, the precarious position?-in which agriculture finds itself at the moment has been dwelt upon at great length by my colleagues and associates, and I feel positive that the gravity of the situation so far as that industry is concerned is apparent to all. I cannot, however, Mr. Speaker, convince myself that the position in which the agriculturist finds himself at the moment is in any sense more precarious, is in any sense less hopeful, than is the position of the Canadian workmen, 200,000 of "whom were out of employment during the early months of this year. There is thiis, however, to be said in the case of the Canadian workman: his condition may be temporary, certainly temporary so far as absolute unemployment is concerned. In the case of agriculture- and I speak particularly of western agriculture-It seems to me that the conditions embody within themselves all the elements that make for permanency; and I hope to prove that a little later in my remarks.
The opportunity has been extended to me for a period of years of coming into association with thousands of agriculturists in the western country and with thousands of Canadian workmen. It has been my privilege to discuss economic questions with them from time to time. During the fall of last year I entered the homes of many industrial workers who were not earning enough at
that time to clothe their children-certainly not enough to clothe them in a way that would enable them to attend school regularly. I know that there are hon. members of this House who will point out to me, and very consistently, the condition in which workmen find themselves in other countries. Naturally I have given some thought to that question, and the comparison would be fair, Mr. Speaker, if we compared this country with other countries somewhat similar in area and population. I have pointed out to those with whom I have discussed these questions that so far as I could discover, so far as I could determine, the only means whereby we could bring immediate relief to these classes-and when I say "immediate relief", I have no thought that my suggestion should prove a panacea for every evil from which they suffer; I have in mind temporary relief in the case of the workmen;-I said to theim that the only means by which temporary relief could be effected would be by increasing the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar. I made that suggestion, Mr. Speaker, believing that when you increase the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar you must of necessity increase the purchasing power of the individual who possesses it. And I thought that by increasing his purchasing power, the extra turnover of goods consumed would more than compensate the producer-that is, the manufacturer- for any loss the readjustment might entail. I pointed out to them also a truth that is self-apparent but which is very frequently overlooked, namely, the inseparable connection between unemployment in this country and the condition in which agriculture finds itself.
During the fall of last year, when unemployment was rampant in the city of Winnipeg, I noticed that upon every train that came into that city there were hundreds of farm labourers, coming in from the farms, helping to swell the tide of unemployment, adding to our city congestion, creating unrest and all the evils associated therewith, the situation was serious, and in discussing its seriousness with the farmers I pointed out the congested condition of the cities. I reminded them of the rents we were paying, and showed how they could help to relieve the situation by keeping the men employed throughout the winter months. I learned that a great many of the agriculturists who up till last winter ordinarily employed anywhere up to five men, were allowing their men to go because the fin-
The Budget-Mr. Hoey

ancial resources at their disposal did not justify their retaining them. Many of them admitted that a large percentage of the labourers were prepared to work through-' out the winter months almost for their board, but they said that their very presence in the home added burdens to the already overburdened farm wife. Together we reached this conclusion, that until the time came when the farmer would feel justified in erecting permanent homes for his hired help, and in that way be able to keep them throughout the year producing enough in the summer to keep them through the winter, we could do nothing to relieve the congestion in the cities during the winter months. But how many farmers to-day are in a financial position to build such homes? I venture to say, not three per cent in the province from which I come. Yet we see the absolute necessity of keeping on these labourers, who year after year reach the cities, so that they can bring up their families in the country in the open air and acquire a taste for outdoor life. If we have in Alberta and Saskatchewan the 55,000 farm homes that are to be found in the province of Manitoba to-day, Western Canada alone will be able to absorb 75 per cent of the men who are now ordinarily unemployed during the winter months in this country.
I sometimes wonder if we are fully seized of the great change that has taken place in western Canada during the last two decades. I am one of those who believe that western Canada would have reached this crisis had we never been engaged in the European conflict. Ten years ago from the public platform I made the statement that we were destined to reach this condition, and nothing has occurred since that day that would incline me to change my view. There were a great many factors contributing to this result, a thousand and one things to which I need not refer at the moment. Less than half a century ago we had a period of nomadic husbandry in western Canada. The pioneers went in there, perhaps the most heroic band of men that ever undertook similar work in any country, and found the land free, taxes negligible, if not unknown, and they started in to make homes for themselves. In those days the West had not been tapped of its resources. It was in those days, it seems to me, that a great many of our present policies were evolved. It was in those days that we evolved and determined our present system of taxation. The quests Mr. Hoey.]
tion in those days was, how much can the West bear? It was a new country where men obtained free land, where labour was cheap because thousands of labourers were reaching this country at that time from Europe, inexperienced men who were prepared to work two or three years for nothing, in order to get experience to enable them to take up farming themselves at a later date, and in those days the question that was asked was, how much can the agriculturalist stand, in the midst of this unlimited wealth, in the midst of these extended natural resources, the finest in the world? It was in those days that we undertook our expensive projects such as the railroads, and political and educational institutions far in excess of the people's needs, far in excess, indeed, of the needs of our present population. So burden after burden was added until I am sometimes afraid, although I trust I am mistaken, that we have added the last straw so far as western Canada is concerned. I have no desire to be unduly pessimistic, but I wonder if we are not living in a fool's paradise when we speak of western Canada and its ability to come back, unless we have a complete reversal of policy in this country.
I said at the outset of my remarks that the conditions in western Canada had been dwelt upon at great length. The trouble with the analysis, as I see it, is that we deal far too much in generalities. I think the time has come when someone should speak, to some extent, scientifically and authoritatively, without bias and without prejudice, and in attempting to do that, while I dislike, to put it mildly, to put these quotations on the official record, there is no doubt in my mind but that they are going to have a profound effect upon land settlement schemes in western Canada in the near future. The statements are authoritative and unassailable. They were prepared by the staff of the Manitoba Agricultural College after an extensive and intensive survey undertaken last year. This memorandum has already been submitted to the Minister of Agriculture in that province, and I have no doubt that a copy has been forwarded to the Minister of Agriculture in this Government. What are the actual facts?
In three decades the average yield of wheat in Manitoba has dropped from nineteen bushels to fifteen bushels per acre.	[DOT]
The criticism frequently advanced that we produce only fifteen bushels per acre, while Germany produces thirty-three bushels per acre, and some other small European countries

The Budget-Mr. Hoey
which import our coarse grains and feed livestock and return the manure from our feeds to their lands get almost as much, is entitled to some defence. The facts are as stated and we must not belittle them, particularly when we remember that with the practice we are following we get only three fifteen bushel crops in four years, or, an actual average of three quarters of fifteen, which is but little over eleven bushels per acre.
The report goes on to say:
The effect of a generation of cropping to wheat has been to reduce the nitrogen of the surface seven inches of soil by 20 to 30 per cent, the phosphorous content up to an equal amount, and the organic matter by from 20 to 50 tons per acre. In other words, in a generation more than one-quarter of the potential wealth of the surface soil has entirely disappeared.
A great deal has been said in this House with regard to the cost of producing wheat. Again we have been dealing largely in generalizations, which, to my mind, are confusing if not misleading. I want to read this item with regard to the cost of producing wheat:
In the survey no attempt was made to arrive at the cost of producing wheat, for the very good reason that this varies with every farmer, every district and every season, and anything less than a thorough study of the cost in different parts of the province and on many different farms extending over a number of years, would be worse than useless, since the figures would be subject to misleading application. No work of this nature has ever been done in Canada, outside of a few counties in Ontario, but some work on cost of production has been done by the Farm Management Department of the North Dakota Experiment Station with the following results:
In the year 1919 the average cost of producing wheat in that State was $2.75 per bushel; the range being from $1.21 to $14.38 per bushel on the different farms studied. In 1920 the average cost per bushel was $2.44; the lowest cost being $1.05, and the highest $3.01 per bushel. In 1921 the average cost was $1.75 per bushel; the minimum 78 cents, and the maximum $5.24.
The above figures for the State of North Dakota, which is not essentially dissimilar in soil or climatic conditions to the Province of Manitoba, should furnish food for thought to all Western Canadian people, particularly when it is recalled that the prices of No. 1 Northern wheat at Winnipeg were as follows-
And this is for the calendar year-
No. 1 Northern, 1919, $2.63
1920,	$1.76 to $2.74
1921,	$1.11 to $1.49
The figures for the years 1920-21 are the highest and lowest monthly prices for the crop year. A much greater proportion of the farmers' wheat was sold at or near the lower prices quoted than was sold at the higher figures. These too are Winnipeg prices. The farm prices were less than these figures by the amount of the freight charges.
Seventeen cents per hundred pounds, I may say, from Winnipeg to Port Arthur.
The farmers' prices were less than these figures by the amount of the freight charges, commission, and other charges for handling. Let me summarize because I think this is of the utmost importance. It is the first scientific attempt that I have been able to discover to determine the cost of producing wheat in western Canada.

It is also interesting to note that the Northwest Territories- this country which I claim has been bearing until now an unnecessary burden-gave that company 18,000,000 acres of land that was free from taxation for a period of twenty years, a period still further extended.

I want to go on and refer to the statement I made earlier in my remarks, that the condition in which agriculture to-day finds itself embodies all the elements that make for permanency. You may reasonably ask what I mean by a statement of that kind? Well, let me refer for a moment or two to the ravages from which agriculture is suffering at this time, ravages that were absolutely unknown-at any rate almost unknown-two decades ago. Let me quote again from the memorandum:
Stem rust has caused an average annual loss of over 5,000,000 bushels of wheat each year, since 1916.
That is in the province of Manitoba.
The lowered production as a result of insect d&predations varies widely from year to year, but is conservatively estimated at seven million dollars per year. In 1921 the Western Wheat-stem Saw Fly alone reduced the yield of wheat in Manitoba by 3,555,000 bushels.
In increased production costs and in lowered yields tihe Manitoba weed crop costs her farmers twenty million dollars per year,-
That is, the wheat crop, on account of the method of farming to which the agriculturalist has been pressed by economic conditions, suffered a loss of $20,000,000 a year in Manitoba.
-or nearly seventy times the annual outlay for the Agricultural College.
Every forty million bushels of wheat shipped out of Manitoba takes from her soil plant food constituents that would cost more than twelve million dollars to replace."
That is what I mean When I say that the condition in which the western agriculturalist finds himself embodies, to my mind, all the elements for permanency. I wish 
to read what these unbiased investigators have to say with regard to rural discontent, because if I referred to rural discontent my right hon. friend to my right would say in reply, "Well, a great deal of the discontent is due to soap-box orators, such as you are," and my words would have no effect whatever. Therefore, I desire to quote what the unbiased investigators say with regard to discontent in western Canada. Their report reads:
Our representatives did the work in the country during June and July last, and while the price of wheat had not at that time reached the low level of later months, it soon became apparent that, even at that time, there was a strong feeling of discontent on the part of many farmers. Generally, they did not complain unduly of their immediate production problems, of soil or climate conditions, or, except in a few districts, of low yields, but the cnief tenor of their complaint was the uneven deflation,-the rapid drop in prices of farm products, and the very much delayed drop in price of most things they had to buy. Among other causes of discontent mentioned again and again were high taxes; high freight rates; the United States tariff on cattle; the high price of machinery; the difficulty of getting help on the farm and in the home, and in some instances the high overhead charges on land and equipment purchased at war prices.
They knew also that increased taxes and transportation charges, and adverse tariff schedules over which they, as individuals had no control, were also contributing causes of discontent ; and they could see no reason why agriculture should be expected to carry, without protest, such heavy losses, while transportation, merchandising and industrial interests delayed post-war deflation.
I desire to repeat what I said, that in view of these conditions I often wonder if we are too optimistic when we speak of the west and1 the ability of the west to come back. I know some hon. members will say, "Well, what about these millions of untenanted lands of which we hear so much?" Well, naturally I have thought of that, and I have discussed the matter at great length with men who ought to know, and they have informed me that these lands that are not to-day populated are almost wholly devoid of plant food elements. They assure me that, if that were not so the lands would have been taken up and cultivated by the farmers who find themselves in an impoverished condition now. A great many of these acres are alkali land. Then, again, they tell me that, where the land is not devoid of plant food content, it is heavily bushed and consequently expensive to clear. Unless, Mr. Speaker, we have a reversal of policy, I cannot see any immediate hope for western Canada. Hon members will ask, what is the solution? We speak a great deal of

The Budget-Mr. Hoey
the tariff. I am in favour of tariff reduction. If I were not in favour of redaction of tariff I would not lie permitted to Sit in this group, hut 1 think the taost drastic tariff reductions are wholly inadequate to meet the situation. We need drastic tariff reductions, or we must close up the west. We also need cheaper transportation facilities'-that is lower freight rate. We need wider markets. They talk of the removal of the cattle embargo as if it were going to usher us into Heaven by the most direct route. I studied the cost of transportation from Moosejaw to Liverpool a year or so ago, when the cattle embargo was the subject of vital interest, and I learned that it took so much to pay the transportation of a steer from Moosejaw to Liverpool that there was nothing left for the farmer who produced the steer, except the tail, and even the tail, in my humble judgment, would have been all twisted. We need drastic tariff reductions, lower freight rates and wider markets. All of these, and the accumulative effect of all of these, are needed to restore agriculture in western Canada. I say-and I am not speaking bitterly or in any partisan spirit-that the economic conditions in this country have forced the farmer, not only to do without a great many conveniences, but to exploit his farm for the time 'being, to exploit the resources of western Canada, and thus forced him to rob future generations of their rightful heritage, and I defy contradiction on that point.
I desire to refer to the statement of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) with regard to the tendency in this country of the people to lean on governments, to come to the government for support, and to seek out governments in order to obtain assistance. I do not think there is any thoughtful Canadian who has failed to notice that tendency in our public life. Next to the tendency of the average man towards cynicism with regard to politicians in this country and political institutions-and we seem to get away from that when we enter practical politics, because even a cynical man has some consideration for our feelings-that tendency to lean on governments, rather than to stand on their own legs, is to me one of the most demoralizing tendencies in the public life of this country. I remember in the country from which I came there were potato crop failures occasionally, and, of course, we subsisted almost wholly on: potatoes. When there was a potato failure, we found ourselves reduced to almost abject penury.
But I remember years when there were failures and some good philanthropist would get together with a government agent with the object of obtaining relief for us. I remember distinctly one year when we were reduced to abject poverty, when men sought relief for the district in which I lived, and when relief was offered in that thickly populated district only two families in the whole district accepted the aid and subsistence that was offered. Why? Because it was humiliating to them to accept government assistance. They had a sense of independence; they did not want government restrictions; their ancestry had fought and fallen for the overthrow of governmental interference. That was the kind of Scotch-Irish stock that built up great civilizations.
But compare that tendency to conditions in Canada to-day. If any man in this country wants to build up an industry, he comes to the government and says: "Will you not prohibit this commodity? It is likely to injure my industry." Another man may not want prohibition, but he may want regulation. I do not believe in governmental enterprises except in so far as they are absolutely necessary. I believe the people should be thrown back on their own individual and collective resourcefulness. I believe the problems of the future will be solved, not by compulsory co-operation, but by voluntary and mutual cooperation. But the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) would have been better advised if he had dwelt at some length upon the cause of which that tendency is the mere outward and visible expression. You ask: Is there a cause? Most assuredly, there is a cause; there is no effect without a cause. What is the basic cause? For many decades in this country we have been making subsidies, subsidies to certain interests at the expense of other interests. How can vou make a subsidy to any interest without penalizing other interests in the country? We have been affording protection to certain interests at the expense of other industris. I have spoken of the lands that are free from taxation in Western Canada. The government of Saskatchewan, a number of years ago, estimated that if the Canadian Pacific Railway were paying taxes in the ordinary way, $300,000 would come into the provincial exchequer every year. Oh, yes, the cause is there all right. Is it not the most natural thing in the world that we should reach a stage in our development when all
233G
The Budget-Mr. Hoey

classes would want to enter the vicious circle? If we are going to protect any industry at the expense of other industries, then let us all get on to the toboggan. The decline is going to be a little more precipitous, but it is going to he exhilarating while it lasts. The same thing exactly is happening in the United States. The farmers there are following in the footsteps of their old friend the protectionist. I am not a very old man, and I may yet live to see the day when my fellow-farmers will be open and avowed protectionists.

Industrial enterprises in that country have, for years, been protected. The United States is gradually becoming a consuming nation, and now the agriculturists see their chance. Honest confession is good for the soul, and I think it is wholesome to make this confession, that agriculturists have no monopoly on altruism. If we afford protection to one industry, why not extend it to all?

speechtext: You cannot.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think I can prove to my hon. friend that you can. We have in southern Manitoba to-day agriculturists who find that, under the most favourable conditions, their lands produce only ten bushels of wheat to the acre. We have in northern Manitoba, in the constituency from which the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) comes, land that produces 35 bushels of wheat to the acre, and which has been producing that regularly for years. Would it not be most reasonable and plausible if the farmers of southern Manitoba came down to the Minister of Finance and said, looking longingly and enviously towards their northern brother: " Give us fifty cents on every bushel of wheat we produce, or we will go out of business." I think they would be perfectly logical; but I think the Minister of Finance would be very well advised in pointing out to them what I have pointed out to them for years, that whereas their land is producing only ten bushels of wheat per acre, it is selling for $18 to $40 an acre, and that their taxes are determined upon that basis; that in the Swan River valley, land is selling as high as $100 per acre cash, and that their taxes are determined by

that value; in other words, that economic phenomena have a flexibility and a levelling process that seem to have escaped completely the notice of our protectionist friends.
Mr. Herbert Spencer in that illuminating essay of his, entitled "Man Versus the State," reminds us of a time in the old country when the farm labourer received one-half of his wages from the farmer and one-half of his wages from the state. Could we not revert to that? Why should the Minister of Finance, in the interest of the unemployed, of whom our protectionist friends speak so eloquently, not revert to the days of which Spencer speaks and have the state pay one-half the wages of every farm labourer? The demoralizing tendency to lean on governments to-day is largely due to the mistaken principle that we have been following for many years in this country, a vicious principle that must lead to its own destruction. I sometimes say: "Let us all get into the circle." Let the snake put its own tail into its mouth and continue to feed. There is all kinds of nourishment before it reaches its head.
I want to refer, in my humble way, to the Fordney tariff as a factor in determining our fiscal policy. Prior to the last election -perhaps I was more conscientious than the average practical politician-that tariff gave me considerable anxiety; and in order to get at the actual facts, at considerable inconvenience I got into touch with three or four of the most outstanding business men in the United States to whom I could obtain access. I discussed the matter with them at some length on my own account; I did so because our platform, the platform that I was advocating, called for radical tariff reductions, and I could not conscientiously stand upon that platform and advocate its principles in view of what was taking place in the United States, until I had further light on the question. What was their explanation? In the fairest way possible they entered into a discussion of trade relations and pointed out to me that they were solidy opposed to the Fordney tariff, not because they had any thought of Canada;-Oh no; not in the least-they were opposed to it because they said it would increase the price of the workers' food. Hard wheat in the United States was becoming expensive, and just in proportion as the food of the worker went up, to that extent his purchasing power of manufactured articles would be limited. And, again, just in proportion as the price of food and the cost of living went up-and

The Budget-Mr. Hoey
they were hoping that it would go down- wages would go up; and they proved conclusively and to my satisfaction that if the American manufacturer ever had an advantage over the Canadian manufacturer by reason of the Fordney tariff that advantage was destined to disappear. They said: "It will not only hamper us in our relations with Canada, but it will give Canada a decided advantage over us in the foreign markets."
Now, in view of that statement, a statement that is reasonable at least, I think that if ever there was a time when we could have made more drastic reductions in the general tariff that time is the present moment. Furthermore, it seems to me that by taking that attitude we would have put an instrument in the hands of the low tariff forces in the United States that would have enabled them, perhaps, to modify the Fordney and McComher tariffs, or any other high tariffs that are likely to displace them. But let us look at the question from another angle. Let us suppose that we have not reached that stage in our development where we can consider matters of trade from that unselfish standpoint. Let us suppose for a moment that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) was actuated by a desire, I will not say to retaliate, because I do not like that word, but just to punish the United States a little for their Fordney tariff. What method could he have followed better than by making a more drastic increase in the British preference? I feel that such would be retaliation with which the right hon. gentleman to my right (Mr. Meighen) would almost agree. I have said a great many perhaps harsh things with regard to the Conservative party and its tariff policy, but I want to be absolutely fair, and I do not think I would be fair unless I made this statement, that throughout their whole tenure of office it is debatable if they ever had as opportune and propitious a moment to make tariff reductions as has this Government at the present time. Certainly there was never a moment in the history of the Conservative party when the time was more opportune and propitious to make such reductions than it is to-day. Let us look at the question for a moment from the point of view of international friction. In view of the Fordney and McComiber tariffs, would we not have been justified in making a radical increase in the British preference without creating any 9 p.m. dissatisfaction in that great country to the south of us that
fought side by side with us in the great crisis? Looking at it from every angle I cannot see any justification whatever for the meagre fare that has been submitted to us. The Minister of Finance has adopted neither one attitude nor the other, and the position he has taken is, to say the least, not intelligible to me in view of present conditions. Our present system of taxation, which bears so heavily upon our working people, which takes eight times as much from the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) as it takes from me, regardless of our ability to pay, if that is the best system of taxation that we can evolve, I cannot see much hope for modern civilization. I want to read an extract from an address delivered by Mr. Lloyd George in the British House of Commons after his return from Genoa. He said:
One of the unfortunate results of the war, which had demonstrated the power of international goodwill, was that it should have developed into narrow, selfish, blind nationalism that was found in every direction-in customs restrictions and in trade and transportation, he declared. Transportation organized to develop international trade was used to prevent international trade. Not merely the amount of tariff was objectionable, he added, but its fluctuations and uncertainties. The human intellect was exhausted in order to make trade as difficult as possible. "This is the condition which we found at Genoa." he asserted.
I wondered, when I read that statement, if the contributions made to the discussions at the Genoa Conference by Sir Charles Gordon, representing the Dominion of Canada, would have any tendency to dispel Mr. Lloyd George's fears and render him more hopeful for the future. Now, someone may say, I suppose, that my address is lacking in the constructive element. A criticism such as that would, I think, have some justification. The critics will no doubt say: "You don't tell us where we are to raise the revenue if we make these drastic reductions". Well, I had in mind that we would raise the revenue from exactly the same sources from which the Liberals contemplated raising it when they framed their 1919 platform. From what source can we extract wealth? From the moon, that burnt out orb, or from the surface of the soil? There is only one way, so far as I can see, that we can meet our financial obligations, and that is by developing our basic industries. We can meet our obligations only by developing our basic industries to the extent that we dream of at this moment, and shipping the surpluses. With the wealth received we could pay off our
The Budget-Mr. Hoey

debts. I am not without sympathy, Mr. Speaker, and I sometimes think that the situation in this country is so serious that it may demand considerable faith on the part of the Minister of Finance. I mean that the Finance Minister might have to have faith enough to bring in a budget that would call for revenues perhaps considerably lower than our expenditure in order to re-establish the basic industry. I do not know; perhaps I have not given the matter enough thought, but I sometimes feel that way when I view the seriousness of the condition of what we ordinarily term the basic industry.
Let me turn for a moment to the amendment-and I do so without any bitterness whatever, in no partizan spirit, with no lust after castigation. I have found the amendment exceedingly difficult to understand, despite the fact that I have inherited all the prejudices that Tory ancestors can bequeath. In order to understand it more fully, I attempted to put myself in the place of hon. members to my right. I found the task exceedingly difficult, but I succeeded to some extent. I tried to look at it from my right hon. friend's point of view, in all fairness, and this is how it appears: the Government went in on a certain platform. That platform was wrong. They made promises that they would embody in legislation the proposals and planks contained in their platform. That is to say, they made a wrong promise. They got into power, but under a sense of responsibility they recanted.
