Then we had the understanding-I will not say there was a promise made-that we were going to have redistribution giving the West the representation to which she wtas justly entitled. We did not have redistribution. I will not call that a broken promise, as it would not be fair, but it was dangerously near it.
I have made the statement, and I made it with no joy in my heart at all, that the party system of government in this country was largely discredited in the consciousness of the Canadian people. I do not want to adopt a holier-than-thou attitude and say that we have discovered something better, but I do say that the Canadian people will never go back to the old by-party system, with its mysterious campaign funds that have exercised such an influence on the policies of this nation. We will never go back to that. We must, if we are true to the living and to the dead, go forward toward something better, something more worthy of us.
Hon. gentlemen to my right are exceedingly anxious to know how we are going to vote. I am going to satisfy their curiosity; I feel the time has come. There is no difficulty in my mind as to how I shall vote. I would not be true to the 
people who sent me here if I did not vote one way-and one way only. No matter what may be the motives that are actuating me in casting that vote-that is a horse of another colour-I am going to vote-and this is the most interesting part of my speech, and I want to state that the whole Progressive group are voting solidly this way-I am going to vote according to the dictates of my conscience, and as a true Canadian with the interests of his country at heart, repudiating broken promises, on the one hand, and political trickery and expediency on the other, voting as a Canadian looking forward to a day when we shall have in this country men whose word shall be as their bond, and who will enable us to build up in this country a civilization that will be a pattern of all that makes for national progress, international comity and good will.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. B. M. BAXTER (St. John city and counties of St. John and Albert) :
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should be less than courteous, and very much less than sincere, if I did not take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), who has delivered his budget on this occasion, on the fact that in the sunset of life he is enjoying the opportunity of again filling a position which he has filled in past years, and which I think the people of Canada will say, without attaching any political importance to the remark, that he has always filled worthily in a personal sense. It would be too much to expect that all the members of this House, let alone the people of Canada, could possibly be in accord with the proposals which the hon. gentleman has to-day laid before the public for acceptance, but it is not too much for us to say that party differences or the differences which are engendered by opposite points of view, commercial points of view, I might call them, should not prevent us from paying a deserved tribute to a worthy Canadian whose life has been full of hard and earnest work. I would like to say, just as a personal appreciation, that it is only during a short time this session that I have had the pleasure of coming in some contact with the hon. Minister of Finance, and I have been delighted to find his extreme readiness of expression, and also to note in every act of his an absolute resoluteness which is too often lacking in the public life of this country. I am glad to be able to say things of this character. If I had criticism to offer, it probably would not be made, because I feel that a long term

The Budget-Mr. Baxter
of public service so distinguished as the hon. gentleman has had ought to entitle him to a very great deal of consideration. I have from a personal standpoint no criticism, but rather an appreciation to oifer.
In discussing the budget proposals I shall try in the short time I intend to occupy the House to approach the subject entirely from what I conceive to be the business point of view. Now my hon friend made use of some figures. I have not the slightest doubt but that they are absolutely correct, and I wish to supplement them with some other figures, because I have already said that the hon. gentleman has shown a resoluteness and courage in dealing with the matters he has laid before the House on this occasion and also, I may say, on other occasions when he has addressed the House. I feel I may digress to this extent: I believe the hon. gentleman is putting forward proposals which by no means go to the length he would like to have them go; they by no means meet his ideal of economic conditions; in fact I may also venture the suggestion that the proposals which he does make on this occasion approach much nearer to the economic ideas of the group of which I am a member than they do those of a large number of the group of which he is one of the exponents. However, he has given us this statement and he has given it, I believe, with absolute sincerity. He occupies the positon which enables him to make this statement because of the success of his party at the polls,-a success which must have been very gratifying to him and to his, party but which was obtained by the violation, in every respect, of that candour and sincerity which distinguishes the hon. gentleman himself. I would pass, for a moment, to a quotation from a speech delivered by the hon. gentleman during the campaign. He said on that occasion:
It would be possible to make the tariff much less burdensome on the people, particularly the poorer classes, without injurying industry, and the Liberals when in power would do this.
I believe the hon. gentleman was sincere when he uttered those words. I take, however, the utterances of his leader (Mrj Mackenzie King) and I am going to quote from a report in the Toronto Globe of a speech made by him in the constituency of York, Ontario. Now, I take it that in public life we had better get down to plain, blunt facts. It is possible, as the late respected Mr. P. T. Barnum said, to fool some of the people all of the time, to fool the
149J
whole of the people part of the time, but impossible to fool all the people all the time. I notice that the leader of the Government assumed in this speech that the population of Canada was nine millions, and I will use that as a basis for testing his calculations and the sincerity of the views put forward, not only by himself on the platform but by his party in their literature, to obtain the adherence of the electorate to that party: assuming nine millions as the population, he said the tax for federal purposes alone would be $62 per head, and for a family of five, $310, a statement that no doubt was read, was noted, and was commented upon by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hoey) who spoke a few moments ago; and no doubt his nerves are still tingling with the idea of this immense burden of taxation. In fact I would not doubt but that his entirely pessimistic attitude with regard to the Canadian West has been more largely inspired by speeches of the character made by the leader of the Government than by the actual facts as they present themselves in western Canada. The leader of the Government further said: that this sum of $310 per year meant the difference between a home and no home, or between giving to loved ones the food or education they needed or not-a most pathetic appeal. And when we look at the figures which have been supplied to us by the Finance Minister, and others which are easily obtained from the records of the country, we find that in the year 1920-21, the year upon which the leader of the Government must have based his calculations, the receipts of the Dominion were something over $434,386,000. That would mean not the large amount of $62 per head but $48.26, and when multiplied by the typical five-member family would come to $241.30. The receipts must surely be the measure of the taxation actually imposed upon this country. If the leader of the Government had used the correct figures I am not going to say it would have made very much difference; but I do say that his appeal was based upon a statement as to the taxation imposed by the late government which was, to say the least of it, absolutely misleading. If, however, |he took the expenditures for the year he would be no more happy because the late government had not spent up to the amount of the revenue and the burden would be $210.30. We come then to 1921-22 when we find that on the basis of the receipts, which is the burden supposedly borne by the

The Budget-Mr. Baxter
five-member family, the tax was $211.80, and on the basis of actual expenditure it was only $193.40.
Now the reason I am commenting on these figures at all is to point out that on the basis of the estimated expenditure put forward by the Minister of Finance this year as the amount-cut to the bone, pared as closely as possible,-the smallest amount he can get along with,-the tax is to be at least $244.85 on the supposed five-member family, or larger than it was under the preceding government. Where then is the relief that was promised on every platform in this country-the relief that was promised to the women of the home in a pamphlet that I have upon my desk and that was largely circulated throughout Nova Scotia; that was promised to every wage earner and to every labourer within the sound of the voice of the leader of the Gov-vernment? One would have expected under those circumstances to have found some real reduction, some real abandonment of expenditure, but instead of that we have an actual increase. Not only have we a failure to implement the pledges-not set out in the platform of the party adopted in convention, but the pledges spoken from the platform and published in the party literature-but there is, as in all other matters, an absolute disregard of them.
I noticed with much attention the attitude taken a few minutes ago by the hon. gentleman who spoke for the Progressive party. He assumed that the party sitting to your immediate left, Mr. Speaker, would be intensely interested in knowing how he was going to vote. I can assure him that that party is only concerned with how it is going to vote itself. We have our principles and we stand true to them. We know how we are going to vote, and we have known for a very long time, in fact, practically, ever since the session commenced, just how the hon. member who has just spoken is going to vote. It was not necessary to volunteer any information on that point. He is going to vote as he voted on the first division this session in this House. He is going to vote in favour of a policy by which a party can go to the country upon a series of misstatements, and if returned to power, he will vote to condone such conduct and will support that party. He talks about what is ethical, and his action drives all that is ethical out of public life. He has quoted the words of the Finance Minister about leaning on governments. I am not particularly concerned with his application of it, but there is leaning and leaning; and

leaning sometimes is a support. We often see a post placed in the road which affords protection to a structure, which would topple over without its support. It is the Government that leans, and it leans for support upon the hon. member who has just spoken.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member tell me, has the Government since its inception ever leaned on the party to which he belongs?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member probably thinks the question is pertinent, and I will tell him that, so far as I know-and he 'has the same opportunity of observing that I have-the Government has never leaned upon the party which sits to the Speaker's left, but I will say that in certain matters the Government members had the good fortune to be possessed of sufficient commonsense to vote the same way as the party which I belong to has voted. That is a Heaven-born gift, that, so far, has been denied to my hon. friend and the party with which he is associated.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is the same commonsense that has influenced me to do it on other occasions.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am quite willing to take my hon. friend's self-sufficient estimate of himself. There can (be nothing much more perfect, probably, in ethics, politics, morality or religion, and we will let it go at that. If the hon. member wants any better character, I will try to improvise one to his satisfaction, but I have no desire for any personal quarrel with him. The leader of the Government went to the country making representations of the character which I have mentioned. Those were public utterances. I have another utterance, where he said that Cape Breton Liberals had fought for the development of the coal and steel industry. I was never aware of any pitched battle on the part of the Liberals for the development of those industries, but, at the same time, that is the statement he made. He also declared that they would continue this fight until they brought back the prosperity Which Canada enjoyed for fifteen years under the Liberal regime, and I notice, as a striking commentary, that my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) told his audiences during the election campaign that a much higher duty should be paid on American coal coming into Canada. Apparently, it was not possible, however, to influence the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to

The Budget-Mr. Baxter
the extent of altering the tariff in the direction of an increase. On that point my hon. friends to the left seem to have had their innings, because the Liberal platform was interpreted throughout the West as meaning abolition' of coal duties, while in Cape Breton, and generally throughout Nova Scotia, it was interpreted as in favour of enhancing those duties, for the protection of that very important industry.
I will refer to a pamphlet issued during the campaign, to which I referred in the debate on the address, in which, I think, a pair of boots was taken as an illustration. The people were assured-the women at all events of Nova Scotia were assured- that it was very wicked of my right hon. friend and leader (Mr. Meighen) to take 50 cents on a pair of boots, of which, I believe, some 20 cents went to the manufacturer, while, if my hon. friend the present leader of the Government were returned to power there would be a difference of some 30 cents in the duty. I said at the time that the thing looked very much like the traditional 30 Cents, 'but I find, after we have had all the tariff proposals, that it does not even reach the munificent sum of 30 cents in the reduction of the cost of living. 1 think about nine cents, after you have calculated1 the duty on an average pair of boots, and after you have taken the increased sales tax, about eight or nine cents, is the amount of the deduction, and you only get that if you import the boots or shoes from England. I am not sorry because I am not advocating the reduction of the duty. I believe in building up the industries of Canada and keeping the workmen within our own country by the produce to be raised, even in this part of the country, which, I am assured, is going very rapidly to the dogs-a statement which I do not accept at all. I want to see our own workmen and our own agriculturalists kept employed. I want to see a united Canada built up. I am glad1 the Finance Minister has not proceeded further in the work of destruction that was promised by his party When out of power.
I think it is entirely a matter of congratulation to the country that the tariff has not been very seriously disturbed, but it is a different matter when the hon. gentlemen who now control the Government and who know the effect of the tariff upon the business of the country, make representations, not only in their platform, solemnly adopted in convention, but also on all the platforms of the country. They made those declarations and stated what
they were going to do. They came into power. They knew just as well before as after they came into power how much money it would take to run this country for a year, and they knew that it could not be done accompanied by any serious tariff reduction. The Finance Minister, with a frankness that is characteristic, told the House and the country what his leader never dared to tell the country, that it is impossible to carry out the pledges that were given in the platform of 1919, and the pledges that were given during the last campaign. That is a manifest fact, and my hon. friend who discussed the matter to-night said over and over again that he was dissatisfied with and humiliated by these budget proposals. He realizes that, according to the Finance Minister, it is an absolute fact that the cost of administering government and carrying on the public services of the country cannot be brought lower, that a burden of taxation must be imposed, and that the only question that remains is as to the distribution of that taxation.
We were promised that a load would be taken off the poor people. We have the pitiful appeal of the leader of the Government, as if people were going without medicine, without food, without education and clothing, because of this tremendous burden of $310 per family, which, after all, is only an average and is not true with regard to any specified family in the Dominion. Yet, that was the nature of the appeal, and now the hon. member who made that appeal had to face the fact that they cannot carry out the promises that they gave, or the suggestions that they made. They cannot, and they dare not, carry into effect the things that they told the people they wanted to do if they came back into power.
How does the case stand with some others? We have already had a vote in this House, and the Liberal party has declared that promises do not bind them; that political platforms are only scraps of paper. The Liberals have informed us that their leader, by a certain magic formula, after the platform was adopted, rendered it as tenuous as some vapour floating over a chimney top. He waved his hands and he uttered the magic words that he accepted all the work that the convention had done, and that he would regard that simply as a chart to be followed, according as he might be advised by those whom he would gather around him into the counsels of the party. Day
The Budget-Mr. Baxter

after day was spent, mile after mile was travelled, health after health was drunk and cheer after cheer was rung around the room for this great magna charta of the Liberal party that was to give us the political and financial salvation of Canada; and yet, when their leader was adopting it, they did not know that he was damning and destroying and tearing it into the veriest shreds and patches and remnants of a policy, a thing not to be followed, not to be carried out.
But there are some other people in this House. Do they stand any better? The Liberal party, like the Conservative party, was repudiated during the campaign by certain other gentlemen. They wanted to stand on the " Mount of Promise " with their faces irradiated with the new political glory. They were going to come down that mount carrying the tables of the new law which would bring a new political salvation into this wretched political sin-struck world. Ah, they broke the tables of the law in carrying them down, just as the other Moses did. According to the other platform, we were to have not a postponed, not a delayed, not a fanciful, but an immediate and substantial all-round reduction of the custom tariff. Did the gentlemen who framed that know what they were talking about? Was this some more vaporous matter to catch votes; or was it the honest belief of the men who penned it and the men who spoke it? What are we trading on in public life anyway? Facts or fallacies, truth or fiction? The decision has to be made here as well as in the country. We can have the immediate reduction as soon as Parliament meets; the hour is now; the opportunity is here; but vigorous and united as they are, and knowing as they say just how they are going to vote, will my hon. friends to my left show me a substantial reduction of any duty, let alone a substantial all-round reduction of the customs tariff? Where is it? They cannot find it themselves, and their friends opposite, their friends in conjunction, cannot and do not pretend to show it to them. Both sides have repudiated the idea of getting any practical, beneficial reduction in the customs tariff; but my hon. friends are going to vote to support a government that gives them this back-handed slap, that destroys their hopes, that repudiates their platform as well as the Government's own.
My friends to my left also solemnly announced to the people of Canada that they were going in for a reduction by 50 per cent of the preferential tariff for Great

Britain. That reduction was to be immediate; that was to be now, not five years from now, and then they were to have further gradual uniform reductions to ensure complete free trade between Great Britain and Canada in five years. I think it is up to my hon. friends to the left to discuss a little less, perhaps, my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen), who has led this party with clearness of vision, with soundness of intellect and with a straight regard every time for the truth and the fact, and to tell us why they stand here mouthing about other things and disregarding their own platform, not daring to stand on the floor of this House and support a single plank or a single atom of the thing they said would bring salvation to Canada. Let those who live in glass houses cease throwing stones; or if they must throw them, let them throw them against a badly shattered glass house just over the way.
That was not their whole platform. Another plank was reciprocity with the United States in natural products. I do not blame them in regard to that; they might have thought they could get that. That might have been an honest mistake; they know now they cannot get it. Another demand was that all foodstuffs should be placed on the free list. Search your free list to-day; search the free list in the tariff proposals of the Minister of Finance, and tell me where you will find foodstuffs on the free list. It will take some searching to find any. Did the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), who leads this party to my left, not know that these things were impossible? Is he such a child that it is only in this session that he has discovered the financial standing of the people of Canada? Is it only now that he learns for the first time that these things cannot be done? Is it possible that he sat in Parliament, in the Government of this country, as year after year went by and he was accumulating knowledge, and yet he had not attained so much knowledge as to know these things were a mere lie, a sham and a deception to the people? Agricultural implements, farm and household machinery, vehicles, fertilizers, coal, lumber, cement, gasoline, illuminating fuel and lubricating oils-all to be free. Show me one of them now; but vote, gentlemen to my left, vote in your morganatic alliance, vote as you told us a while ago that you would. Vote to support, as I said you were supporting, a union always a little shady, a union which gives you none of the benefits, honours or dignities,

The Budget-Mr. Baxter
but which confers upon you any of the degradations that there may be, that puts you to the menial task and takes you not into the household, that seeks you not in the home, but that puts you into a kind of inferior position. But vote for that kind of slavery if you like it.
Raw material and machinery used in the manufacture of these articles were also to be free, and we have the sanction of the great Council of Agriculture upon this. But when we have the budget, my hon. friends across the way, just as much as my hon. friends to my left, cannot refute the fact that was so clearly, plainly, honestly and courageously enunciated by the Minister of Finance, that it takes one hundred cents to pay one dollar of debt; that you have to do that, and that this country cannot go begging. I admire the stand the minister took; I admire his courage. He is about the only man in the two parties who had the courage of his convictions and who has taken hold of matters with a businesslike grasp. He says that you cannot carry out the platform of either the Canadian Council of Agriculture or the Liberal party. But where were the parties before we assembled in this House, before the people did the choosing? Ah, this old party was being blackguarded from one end of Canada to the other as a party of oppressors. From the Atlantic to the Pacific my leader (Mr. Meighen) was termed an autocrat. If there be autocracy in being just; if there be autocracy in telling the truth; if there be autocracy in being honest and four-square; if there be autocracy in not trying to camouflage the situation of the country; if there be autocracy in not begging people for their votes, giving them one kind of coin of political promises in one place and another kind in another-if that be autocracy, then I am more glad than ever that I stepped into the fight and endeavoured to help a man of the character of the leader of this party.
You can review the campaign if you will. Other parties may have things to think about themselves, or about their leaders, or about their press, but there is one thing that cannot be said honestly. It cannot be said that the Conservative party told the country anything else than the thing that it could and would do, the thing that it intended to carry out if it had been returned to power. We did not talk about making everything free and slicing off the customs revenue of the country; we did not talk about lifting burdens off the poor man;
we did not attempt to fool the people for the sake of getting their trust. We were content to come back to power, but only on such conditions that we could face the electorate afterwards and say that we had done nothing other than what we promised, from the platform and from our press, could be done and would be done. We stand therefore in a position of intense satisfaction to-night, when we see our hon. friends to the left prepared to swallow again the dose they took at the opening of the session and stand up here and approve, by their votes and their conduct, the breaking of pledges, virtually declaring that it is not necessary to have any faith or honour in public life at all,
10 p.m. and that all you have to do is to get on a platform and tell the people any old thing that will fool them for a while until the votes are counted, afterwards turning your back on your solemn pledges. My hon. friend who spoke a few moments ago (Mr. Hoey) rather sneered, I thought, at the amendment which has been moved. Let us look for a moment at that amendment. Is there any man in the House who will deny the following statement:
That to these ends, wheat, wheat flour and all .products of wheat; the principal articles of food; farm implements and machinery; farm tractors, mining, flour and sawmill machinery and repair parts thereof; rough and partly dressed lumber; gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils; nets, net twines, and fishermen's equipments; cements, and fertilizers, should be free from customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into same.
Will any hon. member deny that that resolution was adopted? Scarcely. Further, the Liberal party resolved:
That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff.
What hon. member will deny by his vote that the Liberal party adopted that? None, I think.
And the Liberal party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provisions of this resolution When returned to power.
Ah, Mr. Speaker, the prospect of a return to power was the glory of it all,

the hope of power and the realization of power. To proceed:
That such pledges were restated as the policy of the Liberal party in an official handbook issued just before the general election, namely, in October 1921, under the authority of its leader, Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King.
Will any hon. member in this House deny that statement? I think not.

The Budget-Mr. Baxter
That candidates contesting on behalf of the Liberal Party in the said election, used widely the promises therein set out as a means of securing support.
No one, I think, will deny that either.
That the Liberal party having been returned to power, the Budget proposals of the Finance Minister now brought down, constitute, on the part of the Government, an utter failure to implement such pledges by legislation.
Is there a man within the sound of my voice who can say that that is not correct? The Government may offer some excuse for not implementing their pledges by legislation, but they cannot contend for a moment that they have implemented them. They have not implemented one of them. The rest of it follows:
That the making of such solemn pledges, the utilization of them to secure support, and their flagrant violation after tlhe attainment of office reveal a disregard of political honour and tend to lower the standard of public life.
I fancy this is a case where the horse comes up to the hurdle and balks at the jump; for hon. gentlemen know in their consciences that they ought to vote for the amendment. There is not a syllable of it that they can deny. But there is another platform, that of the Canadian Council of Agriculture, that is being equally violated by their supine acceptance of the proposals of the Government, whatever they may be. My hon. friends ought to be congratulated upon the plenitude of their success in this session. One sees the mere wraith of the Wheat Board trailing past the doors and disappearing into the night. There will be no compulsory Wheat Board; not even the bravest of them imagines that now. There will be only the ghost of the Wheat Board to give a warning to certain representatives in the prairies when they next appeal very unwillingly to their assistance. As regards the Crowsnest pass, I do not think my hon. friends are getting very much consolation now that there is some common sense injected into the discussion of that question. Redistribution was another immediate demand on the part of hon. gentlemen, but I think possibly they realize the futilty of repeating that demand this session. By the way, there was an observation made by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) with regard to my right hon. friend and leader (Mr. Meighen) as to redistribution. It is a fact that only about the opening of the session, were the census figures sufficiently completed to enable the House, if it so desired, to consider the question of redistribution, and I should like to know how my right 
hon. friend could possibly have introduced a redistribution bill and got it through before he had those figures or before the census was even taken. When I hear criticism of that kind I am reminded oi the character of men I have canvassec from time to time in the past when I usee to go about soliciting a personal vote. 1 used to encounter a type of man, who, when I asked for his vote, would hit off on something else. There was always something that did not quite suit him. He was dodging the question, and I knew from the start that he did not intend to vote for me anyhow. The hon. member for Springfield will not mind if I class him mentally with those men whom I used to size up as natural born opponents whom I could not win over anyhow. No matter what excuses they made they were bound to vote for the other side. That is the way a great many members of this group regard the hon. member and other vociferous exponents of the Progressive party. After all, they are Liberals. I would not call them good Liberals, because they did not run under the banner of their party; but they thought they had a better chance of getting into the House under the cloak of another party, and another platform a little more deceptive than the Liberal party's, if it is possible to make one so. And now to-day the cloak begins to fall off and we see them in the colours naturally theirs.
I shall not attempt to discuss the budget at any great length. However, there are a few observations that I think it well I should make. Must it not be noticeable to hon. members that right through these budget proposals there is a significant absence of taxation upon luxuries? It strikes at the essentials or fundamentals. Now, let the farmer of this country, to whom the automobile in many cases is simply a replacement of the horse; let such a farmer -I do not mean one of the camouflaged brand who is in politics a Liberal first and a farmer only for principle's sake; I mean the real farmer-let him look at the automobile question. My own view of it is that it would have been wiser in the tariff proposals to treat in a different manner the automobile, say, of the style of the Ford.
I am not going to advocate the use of brother Henry's products in opposition to any other, but I refer to the cheap form of automobile which gives very good service and which to-day has become almost essential to rural life. Why not have helped

The Budget-Mr. Baxter
the man on the farm by refusing to impose excise taxes upon such cars? Why not have taken the broadside that Mr. Attorney General Raney delivered in the last election against undue profits of the Ford Motor Company as at least an excuse for giving to those who need the convenience of an automobile in their business a substantial reduction in the cost of that article? Let the rest of us, those who ride in cars for pleasure, pay the 10 per cent or 5 per cent or whatever it may be, and give to those who really need the automobile some real relief. That is what my hon. friends should have done. I have not heard any of the hon. gentlemen to my left demand that. It is very evident that they are not bothering at all about the farmer; the matter of an automobile to the farmer does not matter.

At all events, we will say it is at least a very gentlemanly tariff; it has proper regard for those who dress in good taste, and the man with collars and cuffs is going to come off better than the
poor chap who has to go to work in his knitted shirt. Well, if my hon. friends to my left want to approve of it, all right. They have the votes; they have the opportunity,-and they also have a splendid opportunity to swallow their vote. I hope they enjoy it; I hope they like to gulf down budget, tariff, principles, everything, for fear that if they voted some other way this Parliament might suddenly go to pieces and they would have to give an accounting of their stewardship to the people of the prairies.
Now, I am not a very belligerent character; at the same time I do not want to be classed as an entire pacifist. I know that what I am going to say will not have very much of Christian savour about it, but I am going to express my real feeling. Perhaps what I say will be much more pagan in its character than hon. members may think it should be. But I should not jest on the subject, because I am in real earnest. Except that it might have cost many thousands of additional lives, I have felt and I always shall feel that the justice of God was not done upon Germany when her cities, her villages and her people remained intact, safe and sheltered, while the land and people of France underwent terrible devastation and suffering. It may not be Christian, but I think it is intensely human to feel that not until we are sure that the brute that is the soul of Germany
for she has no soul-is destroyed, we should not strengthen the power of what was the German Empire. You may trade with her, if you will. If you want to sacrifice everything to commerce; if there is to be no sentiment; if there is to be no feeling in the matter, then we can go on and barter with Germany and let her people do for us the work that the British artisan might do or the Canadian workingman might do near our own homes. If that is your sentiment; if you are willing for the sake of a few cents or a few dollars to let Germany engross your trade, God knows this tariff gives her the opportunity, and she is too only too willing to profit by it. Now, I do not want any one within the sound of my voice or any one who may read what I say to-night to infer for a moment that I desire in the least sense to brand the Government as intending to do anything against our nationality or our British connection, or, above all, in favour of Germany. I would not accuse the Minister of Finance or his colleagues of any deliberate intention in that regard, and I

The Budget-Mr. Baxter
would be very sorry if a thing so cheap and so capable of being used on the hustings as an election cry should be resorted to. I may say that statements of that character have been made about us, and I would not wish a reprisal of them. It is not fair; it does no good to our national life. I would like to see the matter considered on the other basis. Let us, at least, until we are moderately sure that the world is safe, raise a barrier against those countries that tried to kill democracy and slaughter liberty. Let us insist that nothing German, nothing Austrian, shall come in here to be used by our people, not even for the sake of some paltry commercial advantage. If there were a famine in Germany to-night, I would say, let her suffer as a just punishment for the deeds of the past. I would not vote a dollar of Canadian money to send a single ship of relief, to send a single bushel of wheat, even though her population disappeared from the earth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to express to this House my appreciation of the great task which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has undertaken. I do not believe there is a man in Canada in whom the people have greater faith than they have in the present Minister of Finance. In 1896 he gave to this Dominion a budget that brought a period of prosperity that has never been equalled in our history. While the budget perhaps does not go as far as we looked for in the matter of tariff reductions, I am satisfied it is a step in the right direction, and I believe that in the course of time we will eventually get where we want to be. I take this stand: We are in a period of great stress, and the financial condition of this country is such that we cannot put into effect all at once the principles we would like and which we have advocated. Changes must be made gradually, one step at a time, until
[Mr. Baxter.!
we get to the point where it is unwise to go further.
The problem of meeting the expenditure of the Dominion of Canada is a very serious one. The late government, while meeting the expenditure in a way, always failed to raise enough money, with the result that the national debt has been increasing from year to year. In my opinion, the sooner we stop increasing our national debt the better. We simply have to take hold of this question of finance. We should raise as we go along a revenue sufficient to meet our expenses, and I believe the Minister of Finance is making an honest endeavour to solve this problem, which is one of the greatest facing the country to-day, We hear a lot about reducing the expenditure, and that is certainly a wise thing to do. It is easier to reduce our expenditure than to raise money by way of taxation. I think we could reduce the expenditure in some departments of government. I am under the impression that we have a great many more civil servants in the employ of this Government than we need, and if the Government would spend more time in studying the departments with a view to reducing the staffs to the very lowest point consistent with efficiency, I believe they would ultimately come to the point where they would be able to raise a revenue sufficient to cover the expenditure.
At the present time the country is faced with tariffs imposed by other countries. We find that the United States are making an honest endeavour on their part to raise their tariff, and the same is true of practically every country with which we deal. I venture to say that it would be very unwise, much as I am in favour of a low tariff, for the Government at one step to wipe out our tariff against other countries. We must proceed by degrees, and for taking a step in that direction I think the Minister of Finance ought to be commended. While we do not agree with him in all respects I think in the main he is proceeding in the right direction, and we have every reason to follow him with confidence.
The object of every government in this country should be to develop Canada. We have a country with great natural resources. We have stores of wealth that have never been tapped. So far as agriculture is concerned, we have a country which is immensely rich, possibly the richest in the world. We have in the northwest territories perhaps the greatest wheat

The Budget-Mr. W. Elliott
belt in the world, and if we can get settlers of the right class out on that land-only a small proportion of it is under cultivation at the present time-it will help us to pay off our national debt in a way we otherwise could not do.
But the greatest problem before the country to-day to my mind, is markets. Our friends to my right lay great stress upon the home market. There is no one who appreciates the home market more than I do. I represent a constituency in the province of Ontario which has more people to the square mile, I think, than any other rural constituency. I represent the south riding of the country of Waterloo, and we have in that constituency one large city and two or three large towns all within five or six miles of each other. It is a densely populated district. I know and appreciate the value of the home market to the farmer, but unless the home market can consume all the products of our farms, it is practically of no value to us as a means of setting our prices. The prices we get for our farm products are largely fixed by the Chicago and Liverpool markets. They are fixed by our export trade. I believe that one of the greatest things that could be done for agriculture to-day is for the Government to develop markets for agricultural products. Once you get those markets established, you will find no difficulty in settling our idle acres in the northwest. While this is true of agriculture, it is also perfectly true of other industries. I am not one of those who hold the opinion that large towns and cities are a detriment to any country. I know that some of my friends on this side will not agree with me, but I believe the larger our towns and cities grow and the more people we can get into this country, the better it is for we farmers providing-and I make this proviso-that, those cities do not grow at the expense of any other industry. I am just as much opposed to building up agriculture at the expense of industry as I am to building up industry at the expense of agriculture.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have a small population, comparatively, in this Dominion, about eight and three-quarter millions. We speak about the value of the home market, but my contention is that if industry does nothing more than supply the wants of these eight and three-quarter millions of people, it is not going to develop to any great extent. You have to get markets outside. You have to establish markets for the products of your factories in other countries. Some of our friends argue that the way to do that is by keeping up a tariff wall around this country and keeping other products out. I venture to say that that is the surest way to kill the industries of this country. If you want to build up the industries of this country, you must make the tariff just high enough to give us the revenue we require, and not put a great burden on the consumers of this country. Now the same is absolutely true with regard to agriculture; we produce a great many more goods than we can consume. Our friends who advocate a high tariff will say: "Oh, we will supply you with a home market which will consume your products." Well, I do not know that the Canadian people could possibly consume all the wheat that is produced in this country-at least I do not think it would be very good for them if they did. Neither could they consume all the cattle that we produce. We have to get export markets; we have to ship our products out into the markets of the world if agriculture is ever to develop.
I do not intend to deal any further with this question of agriculture, ibut I want to discuss for a few minutes the high cost of living as it affects labour in our towns and cities. To my mind one of the most serious questions which we in this Dominion have to deal with t6-day is the labour problem. We have-very largely, I (believe, as a result of the tariff imposed and the management of the war by the late government-a period of great unemploy-

The Budget-Mr. W. Elliott
ment. We find that we have more unemployed' men in Canada to-day than we ever had before. During the last winter a great many of these men were, for a time, fed at the public expense. Hundreds and thousands of other's, both men and women, were able, by the use of a little money they had saved up, to worry through the winter. Now what is the condition as we find it here today? We find that labour is not being employed as it should be, and that the coming winter will probably see greater hardship brought on the labour people than they have ever experienced1 before, simply because those people are not going to be in the position to stand a second hard year. I think the Government would be well advised to undertake some public work as a relief measure. Ultimately I believe they will have to feed these people; we cannot see them starve. These men do not want charity, they want work; and I believe that ultimately either the provincial or the federal government, or perhaps both, will have to feed this great army of the unemployed during the coming winter.
We find that the cost of living is very little lower than it was before. We find that the cost of coal and the necessaries of life, is very little lower than it was before, with the result that it is almost impossible, owing to the small amount of work which these men have had, for them to exist. Now labour has been blamed for a good many things for which, to my mind, it is not guilty. We have men who, in looking around for a reason for the high cost of living, will tell you to-day that labour is responsible for it. They will tell you that it is because of the high wages they must pay that the cost of living has gone up to its present point. I believe, however, that if we were to analyse the conditions in a great many of our important industries we would find that labour is not getting an undue reward. At the same time, I wish to say that I believe that in some of our industries, in some of our great corporations in the Dominion, labour, perhaps, is too highly paid, and in this connection I refer to the railway corporations. But coming right down to our factories, I spent a good deal of time in two of our industries investigating the conditions of labour. Take the boot and shoe industry, and there are quite a large number of factories in the south riding of Waterloo. We find that labour is blamed! very largely because of the high cost of boots and bhoes. Never in the history of Canada, as far as I can remember, has the cost of the raw material

which enters into the manufacture of boots and shoes been so low. Why, beef hides were actually selling as low as 21 and 3 cents a pound1; they are a little higher now, perhaps in the neighbourhood of 4 or 5 cents a pound, but these prices are very much lower than those paid during the war. Consequently, it cannot be the cost of the raw material that is keeping up the price of boots and shoes.. I have a statement made by the secretary of the Boot and Shoe Workers' Union of Ontario, Mr. O'Dell, of Hamilton, in which he says that the cost of the labour entering into a pair of shoes which retails at $12 is only $1.70. Now, Sir, I maintain that that is not an undue amount to pay for labour ; I believe it is only a fair wage. When we consider further that, according to one manufacturer, 14,000 Canadians engaged in the shoe trade receive an aggregate yearly wage of $10,000,000, this works out at only $715 each. But footwear never cost so much as it does now. Where does the profit go? I maintain that a wage of $715 on the average for the shoe workers in the Dominion is not an excessive wage; and I do not think that any fair-minded man can justly charge labour with being responsible for the high cost of shoes.
Permit me to continue a little further along this line. I have obtained from a very reliable source the cost of the labour entering into the production of a yard of cloth. I might say further that in the south riding of Waterloo we have a number of the finest woollen mills in the Dominion. The figures Which I am going to submit to you with regard to labour are not figures covering one year only, or two years-they are figures covering a period of eight years, so that I think they are fairly correct, and they cover the period in which the cost of woollens was said to be at its very highest. Now, I find this to be the case with respect to the labour entering into the manufacture of a yard of cloth which sells at $2 per yard to the retailer: The labour, represented by the handling, sorting, blending, picking, scouring, carding, gilling, combing, re-gilling, drawing, spinning, twisting, reeling, and so forth, only receives 30 cents, whereas the yard of cloth which that labour produces retails at $2. In other words, for a yard of cloth sold by that firm at $2 per yard the labour cost is only 30 cents. I do not think any of you will say that is an undue charge; and I believe that in this case labour is only receiving a very small part of what it is really worth. You may ask:

The Budget-Mr. W. Elliott
How is it, in view of the fact that labour is getting such a small reward for this work that the cost of clothing is perhaps higher than it has been for years? Now, it takes about 31 yards of cloth to make a suit of clothes, and a little over a dollar, to be accurate $1.12 is paid for the labour which goes into that cloth. No wonder you ask me: " How is it that when we go to buy a suit of clothes manufactured from that cloth, we have to pay somewhere in the neighbourhood of $45 or $50, when the original cost of that cloth to the retailer was only in the neighbourhood of $7?" I venture to say that we never had a greater need for a good active board of commerce in this country to investigate the great cost of these articles than we have at the present time. That is true not only with regard to the articles which I have cited, but of practically every article which goes into human consumption to-day. There is too great a spread between what we get, what the producer gets and what the consumer pays. Until we get down to the bottom of that, we will not solve the question of the high cost of living. I want to be fair and I say that if the tariff on these articles were wiped out completely it would make very little difference in the cost. I have not had time to go into that statement, but I am satisfied it is perfectly true. The cost is somewhere else, and it is the duty of the Government to find out where the excessive cost of the necessities of life comes in.
I will deal now with the question of the tariff. A good number of elections have been won and lost on the tariff. We find that practically every government, both Liberal and Conservative, has used the tariff as a means of winning elections. In the last campaign our friends to the right said the tariff was the only issue. Well, it did not work out very well, as far as they were concerned. They lost the election, and our friends on the other side of the House won. Now, stripped of all its mystery, very few people thoroughly understand the tariff. We have a plank in the platform of the United Farmers, which is also incorporated in the platform of the Independent Labour party of Canada, which reads:
That the tariff should not be a political football to be kicked about for election purposes, but should be placed in the hands of a qualified and representative commission, whose duty it should be to administer the tariff in a scientific manner, Labor then having an opportunity to protect its interests.
This was taken from the Labour platform, and further on-
That every claim for tariff protection by any industry should be heard publicly before this proposed commission.
Another plank in the platform reads:
That all corporations engaged in the manufacture of products, protected by the customs tariff, be obliged to publish annually comprehensive and accurate statements of their earnings.
I believe in that plank, and I think there are very few members in the House of Commons who know enough of the tariff to say definitely whether any industry needs protection or whether it does not. I have great respect for the high calibre of the members of this House, but, nevertheless, in order to state definitely that any industry is in need of protection, we must spend a good deal of time investigating the question, and I believe in the appointment of a commission to investigate it. That commission should be composed of men who were above reproach, and beyond the possibility of any outside influence being brought to hear on them. It would also be a representative commission, composed of a representative of agriculture, and a representative of labour. I would not say that we should have a representative of every industry, because that would be going a ' little too far. With a commission such as this, inquirying into the conditions as we have them to-day in the country, I believe we would get the very best information possible regarding our industries. I do not say that this commission should be independent of Parliament. It should be appointed under Parliament, and only for the purpose of making recommendations to Parliament. Those recommendations would be acted upon, and Parliament would have to assme the responsibility of those recommendations, if they were put into effect. The second clause in this platform, which I consider of great importance, reads:
That every claim for tariff protection by any industry should be heard publicly before this proposed commission.
I believe that if this commission were in operation we would get a very great amount of information which would be valuable to the people of Canada. We would find out a lot of things which would be a great surprise to us. We have been told in the past that a great many of our manufacturers have been making immense sums of money. We have been told that the Dominion Textile people made a profit of 310 per cent in one year. I do not
The Budget-Mr. White

know whether that is true or not. It has been stated on public platforms and never denied, as far as I have heard. It would be the duty of this commission to inquire and find out whether that firm had been making such undue profits in one year or not.
With regard to the woollen industry I have been told-in fact the evidence which I have at the present time bears out the statement-that for a period of ten years the average profits of the woollen industry of Canada have been in the neighbourhood of 5 or 6 per cent. I do not know whether that is true or not, but it would be the duty of the commision to find out, and once they had that knowledge, and once they had all the cards on the table with regard to any particular industry, the commission would be in a position to say whether that industry required any assistance or not in the way of a tariff. However, with regard to any of our industries which are native to Canada, if upon an examination of their statements before the commission it is proven to the commission that they require protection, I would be in favour of giving them protection. We find that other countries are adopting this system. We found out just the other day that the United States made a move in this direction. While I do not believe in following . the lead of United States in every particular, yet it is an indication that the people of other countries are thinking along these lines, and I think if the Government would adopt such a system as a tariff commission, which is one of the planks in our platform, they would receive a good bit of support from this side of the House. The tariff is more or less of a mystery to me, I am free to confess. I suppose I have a fair amount of knowledge upon it, yet I believe the Government is justified in dealing carefully with it. I do not think they would be justified in making any undue reduction, owing to the present unsettled state of this country. I think the action of the Government, while it is not all we desire, is, at least, commendable and goes in the right direction.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think a repetition of congratulations to the hon. Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) is hardly

necessary and somewhat tiresome. I can only say that I admire the Finance Minister for the pluck he has shown in facing a very difficult proposition, and that I wish him many years of the vigour, both of body and mind, which he now enjoys. I could not help thinking, as I heard his budget speech, that another milestone had been passed in the matter of election pledges, promises and arguments. I remember that in the days gone by we have heard of commercial union; we have heard of free trade as they have it in England; we have heard of tariff for revenue only, of reciprocity; and now we have the first outcome of the Liberal tariff platform of 1919 with its solemn pledges and its chart and compass attachment. As to what the final1 outcome will be, I suppose it is a case of, no man knoweth. If we consider the proposed tariff changes by themselves, there is some slight reduction; but if we consider them in connection with the 50 per cent addition to the sales tax, the reduction is so slight as to be almost invisible. Some have said that it is a step in the right direction, but I think such hon. gentlemen are quite satisfied with a very short step. It is rather significant that the budget does not contain any new sources of revenue. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has not been able to tap any fresh source; he has simply added to those which we have had before, and it seems to me that this is quite a compliment to the previous Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) and the late government. In the case of these slight tariff reductions, I would point out that Canada is the only nation that I know of which is reducing tariffs. In the last two or three years, the customs tariffs of most countries have been increased, and it might be said that all the world, excepting Canada, is opposed to a reduction of tariffs.
Since coming to this House, I have been very much interested in the speeches of the party to my left, and the Ontario members, who number about one-third of that party, have been strangely silent upon many subjects. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) to-night gave quite a blue picture of the golden West, about the bluest that I have ever heard. We have just listened to the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Elliott), who, I believe, advocated before the election the tariff commission that he has spoken of to-night. He also says that he is in favour of a tariff for revenue. I was just wondering, if a few more of the Ontario members of

The Budget-Mr. White
that party would express their views, whether we would not have just about as cosmopolitan a membership in that party as there is in the Liberal party. It was somewhat to my surprise that he cleared the manufacturers of cloth of any duplicity or any arrangement whereby prices were hoisted to too high a level.
We had before the special Railway Committee a day or two ago the Hon. George Langley who, in giving evidence before that committee, said that the western country from which he came, had lost confidence in a certain commission. We have had the Railway Commission looking after railway matters for some years; and if a certain section of the country loses entire confidence in the Railway Commission, why cannot other sections of the country lose confidence in a tariff commission? The tariff is too intimately connected with our raising of revenue to be entrusted to a commission.
We have heard a great deal about the troubles of hon. gentlemen to the left, and it seems to me that some of those are troubles which no legislation can remedy. They had bad weather conditions during the last two years, and I would point out that no Act of Parliament can command the velocity or the direction of the wind, or the downfall of rain or the time at which it shall come. It seems to me that while climatic conditions may not be ideal, the greatest trouble they have and the greatest drawback to their success is the exorbitant freight rates which they are compelled to pay. We are told that the special Railway Committee will have something of interest and of value to bring before this House when they are ready to report. Probably another reason for some of their troubles is, that dry areas in the southern part of Alberta and Saskatchewan were opened up for farming, when they might better have been left as grazing country and would probably have produced more than they have under cultivation. Although members of that party are opposed to protection in all its forms, or at least some of them are, we have heard from one to-night who is not. Some hon. members have explained that they are not asking for any special protection or special privilege; but they are willing to vote large sums for the promotion of the interest of agriculture, and I do not object to that. They are quite willing to ask for a wheat board, and in the present progress that the wheat board is making, I have my doubts whether it
will be of any use to them. But if that is the regulation they want, I am quite free to say that I am willing to support that measure.
I have looked up the record of importations of farm produce, and I find that, in the year ended March 31, 1921, under nineteen items there was imported into this country the produce of farms to the value of $71,500,000. It seems to me that there is food for thought in those items. For instance, we imported 3,741,000 pounds of butter, of which 2,207,000 pounds was received from the United States. We exported 9,739,000 pounds, nearly 6,000,000 of which went to the United States. I am giving the figures in round numbers. The United States duty is now 6 cents a pound. Under the regulations now before the Senate, I believe it is proposed to raise it to 8 cents. The Canadian duty is 4 cents per pound.
Of eggs in the shell, we imported 5,342,000 dozen, of which 5,201,000 dozen came from the United States. That does not take into consideration eggs in the frozen state. We exported 6,579,000 dozen, of which only 191,000 dozen went to the United States. Eggs were admitted to the United States free. The proposed tariff is 8 cents per dozen. The Canadian duty is 3 cents per dozen.
We have heard a great deal about efforts being made to secure wider markets; and while I would not minimize those efforts, I would say that it behooves us to examine these conditions, to find out the reason why these things exist and to take steps to secure our own markets to ourselves. The home market is the most valuable market we have; it is the most stable, and it is the one that will stick by us in the end.
As to the free trade view of some members of the party to our left I might remind the House that we have experimented somewhat with that policy. During the stress of war, when the necessity for the production of foodstuffs was so great, the government of that day, in order to encourage such production, placed farm tractors on the free list. They did so with the best intentions, by a temporary provision under an Order in Council. Now, in 1919 and 1920 there were imported from the United States tractors to the value of some $20,000,000. The people of Canada paid the duty on those tractors in the form of exchange. They paid to the United States an exchange that averaged 14 per cent during all that.time, and that money
The Budget-Mr. White

went to keep the American factories busy, and to keep open the channels of their trade. When the transaction was completed we had the tractors and the Americans had the cash. Those tractors might have been made in Canada, and we would have had the tractors and the cash as well.

speechtext: Is it not a fact that a large proportion of the money Canada has invested in the banks to-day is loaned to industries operating in the United States at the present time?

CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is the hon. member
aware that the dye industry in Great Britain is agitating for a repeal of that tariff?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have not heard of that, but I am aware that the agricultural industry in Great Britain is opposed to the removal of the cattle embargo.
Perhaps the most important announcement in the Budget is that which deals with the duties on articles coming from countries that have a depreciated currency. The minister referred to the tariff which has existed up to the present time as a tariff of 1,000 per cent. I wonder how he figures the present tariff. Take an article that cost 100 marks, with a duty of 30 per cent added. With undepreciated exchange that article would be worth, in round figures, $24. A thirty per cent tariff would mean a duty of $7.20. The previous method of figuring would bring it to $3.60. With the present method of calculating on the depreciated currency, that article, instead of bearing a duty of $3.60 as formerly, would bear a duty of 10 cents. I think, therefore, that the statement that we are going to have free trade with Germany is not wide of the mark. Now, under our immigration regulations we keep out the German and Austrian artisan and labourer. We say that they shall not come here and take the work from our Canadian citizens. Yet, when the products of their labour come to us in the shape of German goods we let them in practically free of duty. The minister gives as a reason for this change that the previous regulation was broken. Is it not a fact that almost all laws on the statute books are broken? But would he advance that as any justification for repealing all laws? The plain duty of the Government, it seems to me, was to amend the regulations which are not satisfactory, to make them stronger and more drastic, thereby giving the Canadian workman and manufacturer some protection from the workmen who produce these foreign goods in countries where the standard of living is low. The abolition of the depreciated currency

Questions
regulations comes at a time when we have a great deal of unemployment, and when many of our factories are running on short time, in common with most other countries. We also have many soldiers who are out of work, some of them marching to Ottawa to put their case before the Government. No doubt the war has unsettled a good many of them, and possibly some were not employable before the war. The putting on of the khaki did not make them saints, but it cannot be denied that the great majority of them would make good if given proper conditions. Now, this very small duty on the German goods is practically no protection, so that almost the only protection we have left is sentiment. Sentiment will keep many of these manufactured goods out of the country, but they will come in in camouflaged form and the people will not know, when they are buying, where the goods were made.
The other day when the militia estimates were under consideration, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), a returned soldier, I believe, attacked them quite successfully. I have been wondering whether he will speak up in protection of his former comrades when this matter of depreciated currency comes up-whether he will do his best to see that the soldiers and the unemployed get justice. Personally, I saw Canada's men march out in the pride of their youth and strength. I saw some of my best friends go with them and I heard afterwards that they had been done to death in the most hideous fashion. I saw some of them come back broken in everything but their spirit, and I saw others return who seemed to be in good health, but whose experiences will mean that they will not live out half their days. I am free to confess that I have not reached that state of grace where I can welcome a would-be autocratic German or the goods which he manufactures. I contend, Sir, that the Government has not done its duty by the Canadian people, who are anxious to maintain their present standards of living, nor has it, in particular, done its duty by the men who sacrificed so much that the liberty we believe in might not perish from the earth.
On motion of Mr. Kyte the debate was adjourned.
